odd-extensions.four-extensions-oriented-.formal:
The single extensions of this world and its mirror are, with their residues,
\[
\begin{array}{lllll}
\toprule
\text{extension} & \text{algebra} & \omega^{2} & \text{structure} & r \\
\midrule
\text{this world} + \text{space} & \Cl(1,4) & +1 & \Cl(1,3) \oplus \Cl(1,3) & 5 \\
\text{this world} + \text{time}  & \Cl(2,3) & -1 & \Cl(1,3) \otimes \C \cong \Mat(4,\C), \ \Cl^{0} \cong \Cl(3,1) & 7 \\
\text{mirror} + \text{space}     & \Cl(3,2) & +1 & \Cl(3,1) \oplus \Cl(3,1) & 1 \\
\text{mirror} + \text{time}      & \Cl(4,1) & -1 & \Cl(3,1) \otimes \C \cong \Mat(4,\C), \ \Cl^{0} \cong \Cl(1,3) & 3 \\
\bottomrule
\end{array}
\]
In both towers the generator of the time sign complexifies and the generator of the space sign doubles. In the complexified rows the complex unit is the extension's central volume element $\omega$ ($\omega^{2} = -1$, commuting with every vector; $\omega = \pm I_{5}$ for $\Cl(2,3)$, Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), not the shadow's pseudoscalar $e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}e_{4}$. The labels follow the uniform convention (time a generator of square $+1$, space one of square $-1$, in both towers); in T14's causal convention the mirror's time is its minus sign, so its space and time extensions are $\Cl(4,1)$ and $\Cl(3,2)$, each the reversal of ours of the same kind, and the convention-free rule is that a generator of square $-1$ doubles and one of square $+1$ complexifies (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.mirror-extensions-causal-convention}).
odd-extensions.four-extensions-oriented-.technical:
The single extensions of this world's $\Cl(1,3)$ and the mirror's $\Cl(3,1)$ are: this world plus space, $\Cl(1,4)$ with $\omega^{2} = +1$, doubled to $\Cl(1,3) \oplus \Cl(1,3)$, residue $5$; this world plus time, $\Cl(2,3)$ with $\omega^{2} = -1$, equal to $\Cl(1,3) \otimes \C \cong \Mat(4,\C)$ with even part $\Cl(3,1)$, residue $7$; mirror plus space, $\Cl(3,2)$ with $\omega^{2} = +1$, doubled to $\Cl(3,1) \oplus \Cl(3,1)$, residue $1$; mirror plus time, $\Cl(4,1)$ with $\omega^{2} = -1$, equal to $\Cl(3,1) \otimes \C \cong \Mat(4,\C)$ with even part $\Cl(1,3)$, residue $3$.

In both towers the time generator complexifies the shadow and the space generator doubles it. These labels are the uniform convention; in T14's causal convention, where the mirror's time is its minus sign, the mirror's two rows exchange labels and become the reversals of ours.
odd-extensions.four-extensions-oriented-.lay: Our spacetime algebra and its mirror image can each be extended by one extra direction, of time type or of space type, giving four algebras. Adding a space direction produces two identical copies of the original algebra side by side, while adding a time direction produces the original algebra with complex numbers allowed. Each of the four lands on a different odd value of the series' mod-eight charge.

proofs.main: Both shadows have $q$ odd ($3$ and $1$); a time generator leaves $q$ unchanged and a space generator raises it by one, so by Lemma \claimref{odd-extensions.volume-element-odd-dimension} the time extensions have $\omega^{2} = -1$ and the space extensions $\omega^{2} = +1$, and Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification} gives the structures. The even subalgebras are from Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(iii): $\Cl^{0}(1,4) \cong \Cl(1,3)$, $\Cl^{0}(2,3) \cong \Cl(3,1)$, $\Cl^{0}(3,2) \cong \Cl(3,1)$, $\Cl^{0}(4,1) \cong \Cl(1,3)$. The residues are $p - q \bmod 8$. The identification $\Cl(1,3) \otimes \C \cong \Mat(4,\C)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.sta-matrix}) is Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-representatives-dimension-nearest-four-types} complexified.

odd-extensions.imported-towers-clock.formal: The $(1,1)$ ascent $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p+1,q+1) \cong \Mat(2, \Cl(p,q))$ preserves $p - q$; the real Clifford algebras are periodic modulo eight; the eight residues label eight parallel towers. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thms.~3.2 and 3.6]{ButlerT3}; \cite[Fact~2.5]{ButlerT14}.
odd-extensions.imported-towers-clock.technical:
The $(1,1)$ ascent $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p+1,q+1) \cong \Mat(2, \Cl(p,q))$ adjoins a hyperbolic plane and so preserves $p - q$, and the real Clifford algebras are periodic modulo eight. The residue $p - q \bmod 8$ therefore labels eight parallel towers, each closed under the ascent.

In the store this fact restates the tower's commuting-copies and rigidity results and the corresponding dark-matter fact.
odd-extensions.imported-towers-clock.lay: The series' completion step adds two directions of opposite sign, which turns the algebra into two-by-two matrices over itself and leaves the difference between the counts of the two kinds of direction unchanged. Real Clifford algebras repeat with period eight in that difference. So the algebras fall into eight separate towers, and climbing never moves between them.

odd-extensions.imported-towers-clock.typing_note: The three uses are exactly the cited provenance and are kept; mod-8 periodicity is classical but no imported periodicity claim exists in the store, so no standard-route derivation was added.

odd-extensions.mirror-inside-complexifie.technical:
In $\Cl(2,3)$, this world's time extension with $Q(e_{5}) = +1$, the generators $e_1, \ldots, e_4$ generate a copy of this world's $\Cl(1,3)$, while the bivectors $e_\mu e_5$ anticommute pairwise with squares $(-1,+1,+1,+1)$ and generate the whole even subalgebra, a copy of the mirror's $\Cl(3,1)$. The two copies meet exactly in $\Cl^{0}(1,3) \cong \Mat(2,\C)$, of dimension eight, and $\Cl(2,3) = \Cl(1,3) \oplus \omega\,\Cl(1,3)$. No automorphism of $\Cl(2,3)$ carries one copy onto the other: the natural map $e_\mu \mapsto \omega e_\mu$, a Wick rotation reversing each square, is complex-linear and not an automorphism of the real algebra.

In the space extension $\Cl(1,4)$, with $Q(e_{5}) = -1$, the generators $e_\mu$, the bivectors $e_\mu e_5$ and the elements $\omega e_\mu$ all generate copies of $\Cl(1,3)$, and $\Cl(3,1)$ admits no unital embedding into $\Cl(1,4)$. The mirror's two extensions behave the same way with $\Cl(1,3)$ and $\Cl(3,1)$ exchanged.
odd-extensions.mirror-inside-complexifie.lay: When our spacetime algebra is extended by an extra time direction, the mirror world's algebra appears inside the result, sharing with ours exactly the part that describes Lorentz rotations and spinors. Even so, no symmetry of the enlarged algebra turns ours into the mirror's; the link between them is a Wick rotation, which needs complex numbers. When the extra direction is of space type instead, the mirror's algebra cannot be found inside at all.

proofs.main:
(i) is the definition of the shadow. (ii) is Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(iii) with $e_{5}^{2} = +1$: the products square to $-e_{\mu}^{2}$, which is $(-1, +1, +1, +1)$, and generate a subalgebra of dimension sixteen inside the even subalgebra of dimension sixteen. (iii) The shadow's even part consists of even elements of $\Cl(2,3)$, so it lies in the intersection; the shadow's odd part consists of odd elements of $\Cl(2,3)$, since the generators $e_{1}, \ldots, e_{4}$ are odd there, so it meets the even subalgebra in zero; the intersection is exactly $\Cl^{0}(1,3)$, of dimension eight, and $\Cl^{0}(1,3) \cong \Cl(3,0)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.sta-matrix}) $\cong \Mat(2,\C)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.pauli-algebra}) is the Pauli algebra. For the spanning statement: $\omega$ times a blade of the shadow is, up to sign, the complementary blade of the shadow times $e_{5}$, so $\Cl(1,3) + \omega\,\Cl(1,3)$ contains every blade of $\Cl(2,3)$ (the script checks the dimension); this is the shadow's version of Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(ii), which decomposes by the even subalgebra instead. (iv) An automorphism carries a subalgebra to an isomorphic subalgebra, and $\Cl(1,3) 
ot\cong \Cl(3,1)$ by Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-representatives-dimension-nearest-four-types}. With $\omega$ central and $\omega^{2} = -1$, $(\omega e_{\mu})^{2} = -e_{\mu}^{2}$ and the $\omega e_{\mu}$ anticommute pairwise, so they generate a $\Cl(3,1)$; this is the complex-linear identification of the two real forms and it is not an automorphism of the real algebra, since $\omega e_{\mu}$ is a $4$-blade, not a vector.

For $\Cl(1,4)$: Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(iii) with $e_{5}^{2} = -1$ gives $(e_{\mu}e_{5})^{2} = e_{\mu}^{2}$, and $\omega^{2} = +1$ gives $(\omega e_{\mu})^{2} = e_{\mu}^{2}$, so all three sets generate $\Cl(1,3)$. For the non-embedding: $\Cl(1,4) \cong A \oplus A$ with $A = \Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat(2,\HH)$ by Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(i) and Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-representatives-dimension-nearest-four-types}. A unital homomorphism $\phi: \Mat(4,\R) 	o A \oplus A$ composed with the projection to a summand on which $\phi(1) 
eq 0$ is a unital homomorphism $\Mat(4,\R) 	o A$; its kernel is a two-sided ideal of the simple algebra $\Mat(4,\R)$ not containing $1$, hence zero; so it is injective between real algebras of equal dimension sixteen, hence an isomorphism, contradicting $\Mat(4,\R) 
ot\cong \Mat(2,\HH)$ (Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-representatives-dimension-nearest-four-types}). The statements for the mirror's extensions follow by exchanging the roles of $p$ and $q$ throughout. The script verifies the squares, the anticommutation, the dimensions of the generated subalgebras and of their intersections with the even subalgebra, and the Wick-rotated squares, for all four extensions.

odd-extensions.two-readings-which-which.formal: The two readings of $\Cl(1,4)$ that occur in the series are two solderings of one algebra, and the series' definition of the residue assigns them to different towers. The fifth direction of the frozen point's algebra is not a spacetime direction and never was: it is the Stelle-West vector, the normal to the de Sitter hyperboloid, with fixed norm $\ell = \sqrt{3/\Lambda}$, and its algebra is this tower's. The five-dimensional dark towers, if populated, are soldered to a fifth tangent direction that the frozen point does not supply, whose size $L$ remains the datum the series does not fix. Proposition \claimref{odd-extensions.four-extensions-are-four-odd-towers} therefore holds as a statement about algebras, and only about algebras.
odd-extensions.two-readings-which-which.technical:
The two readings of $\Cl(1,4)$ that occur in the series are two solderings of one algebra, and the residue, read from the soldered space, assigns them to different towers. The fifth direction of the frozen point's algebra is the Stelle-West vector, the normal to the de Sitter hyperboloid with fixed norm $\ell = \sqrt{3/\Lambda}$; it is not a spacetime direction, and that algebra belongs to this tower.

The five-dimensional dark towers, if populated, are soldered to a fifth tangent direction that the frozen point does not supply, of a size $L$ the series does not fix. The identification of the four single extensions with the four odd towers therefore holds for algebras, and only for algebras.
odd-extensions.two-readings-which-which.lay: The same five-dimensional algebra turns up twice in the series with two different meanings. In one, the fifth direction is the fixed radius direction of de Sitter space, which belongs to our world; in the other it is a genuine extra direction of a hypothetical dark sector, whose size the series leaves open. Matching the single extensions to dark towers is therefore a statement about the algebras alone.

odd-extensions.two-towers-one-curved-uni.technical:
Both oriented towers are soldered to the one gravitational field on flat spacetime, the mirror reading its derived metric with the sign reversed, so the mirror's tractor bundle has signature $(4,2)$ and its frozen point has norm $-Q(I)$. In de Sitter the intermediate algebras are the doubled $\Cl(1,4)$ for this world and the complexified $\Cl(4,1)$ for the mirror; in anti-de Sitter they are the complexified $\Cl(2,3)$ and the doubled $\Cl(3,2)$. The even subalgebras $\Cl^{0}(1,4)$ and $\Cl^{0}(4,1)$ share one presentation, so the two towers' spin groups, spinor modules and MacDowell-Mansouri bivector algebras coincide, and the derived content of the copy theorem does not see the doubling.

What differs is the bare fifth generator alone: $Q(e_5) = -1$ with $e_5 = \pm\omega'$ on the two summands when doubled, against $Q(e_5) = +1$ with $e_5 = \omega'^{-1}\omega$ when complexified. That generator is the unit vector along $V$, outside the soldered space and in the pure-gauge sector, so the sign of $\Lambda$ distinguishes the towers' intermediate algebras without selecting which tower is visible.
odd-extensions.two-towers-one-curved-uni.lay: Our world and its mirror share one gravitational field on a flat background, the mirror with the sign of every squared distance reversed. The sign of the cosmological constant decides which of the two gets the doubled form of the halfway algebra and which gets the complex form. But everything the series derives from these algebras is the same for both, and the one element that differs points along a direction that is not part of spacetime and carries no physical fluctuation, so the sign of the constant does not pick out which world is the visible one.

proofs.main: The metric $g$ below is the derived metric $g(a,b) = \hb^{-1}(a) \cdot \hb^{-1}(b)$ of the gravitational field and $-g$ the mirror's reading of it; its Levi-Civita connection, Ricci tensor and scalar curvature are read from $\Omega$ and $\mathcal{R}$ by Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(ii) and (iv). (i) The tractor bundle of a conformal class of signature $(p,q)$ carries a metric of signature $(p+1,q+1)$ (Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-frozen-point}), so the class $[-g]$ of signature $(3,1)$ has a tractor metric of signature $(4,2)$; in a scale $g$ the tractor metric is $2\sigma\rho + g^{-1}(\mu,\mu)$ and the scale tractor of $\sigma$ is $(\sigma, \nabla\sigma, -(\Delta\sigma + J\sigma)/n)$ with $J$ a multiple of the scalar curvature; under $g \mapsto -g$ the Levi-Civita connection and the Ricci tensor are unchanged while the inverse metric, the Laplacian and the scalar curvature change sign, so $\rho \mapsto -\rho$; the map $\Phi: (\sigma, \mu, \rho) \mapsto (\sigma, \mu, -\rho)$ from the tractor bundle of $[g]$ to that of $[-g]$ is scale-independent, intertwines the two tractor connections, carries the scale tractor of $g$ to that of $-g$, and satisfies $h_{-g}(\Phi X, \Phi X) = -h_{g}(X, X)$. Hence the mirror's frozen point has norm $-Q(I)$ and its $I^{\perp}$ has the reversed signature of ours: $(4,1)$ against $(1,4)$ and $(3,2)$ against $(2,3)$; the doubling or complexification is Corollary \claimref{odd-extensions.four-extensions-oriented-pair}. (ii) Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(iii): with $e_{5}^{2} = -1$ in $\Cl(1,4)$ and $e_{5}^{2} = +1$ in $\Cl(4,1)$ the products $e_{\mu}e_{5}$ square to $e_{\mu}^{2}$ and $-e_{\mu}^{2}$ respectively, which are both $(+,-,-,-)$ since the two Lorentz frames are reversed; a Clifford algebra is determined by such a presentation. That the copy theorem's inputs are spin-group objects is Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-copy-theorem-soldered-residue}. (iii) is Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(i) and Remark \claimref{note.odd-extensions.added-axis-pseudoscalar}. In the closing clause, the unit vector along $V$ lies outside the soldered space by Proposition \claimref{odd-extensions.belongs-tower}(i) and in the pure-gauge sector by Fact \claimref{dark-energy.point-infinity-has-no-physical-fluctuation}. The script verifies the signatures of the mirror's $I^{\perp}$ on the same rational instances, the two-by-two rule from the signs of $\omega^{2}$, the common presentation of the even subalgebras, and the squares and factorisations of $e_{5}$.

q.tower.odd-charge.formal: For $p - q$ odd the connecting twist is outer on the centre and Lemma \claimref{tower.grade-twist-when-it-inner} fails; the limit is still an AF-style object (an increasing union of finite-dimensional semisimple algebras), but its identification is sensitive to how the twist moves the two central idempotents (split case) or conjugates the complex structure (complex case). Identify $\varinjlim T_k$ for odd charge; in particular decide whether it is again a plain tensor product with $\Mat_{2^\infty}$, and what real K-theoretic invariant separates the cases if not.
q.tower.odd-charge.technical:
For odd transport charge $p - q$ the connecting twist acts as an outer automorphism on the centre, so the lemma that makes the grade twist inner in the even case fails. The direct limit $\varinjlim T_k$ is still an increasing union of finite-dimensional semisimple algebras, but identifying it depends on how the twist moves the two central idempotents (split case) or conjugates the complex structure (complex case).

The question asks for that limit: is it again a plain tensor product with $\Mat_{2^\infty}$, and if not, which real K-theoretic invariant separates the cases?
q.tower.odd-charge.lay: For towers of even charge the series knows exactly what the infinite limit of the ladder of algebras is. For odd charge each step twists the centre of the algebra in a way that blocks the same argument. The question was what the limit is in that case, and whether some invariant from K-theory is needed to tell the possibilities apart. It is settled: the limit is again a plain tensor product, now of the even half of the starting algebra, and it is the same algebra for every tower, so no invariant tells the cases apart.

rungs.imported-tower-one-qubit-per-rung.formal: The transport principle completes $\Cl(p,q)$ to $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ by adjoining one hyperbolic pair, and the completed algebra carries a null cone of its own, so the completion iterates: the $k$-th rung is $T_{k} = \Cl(p{+}k, q{+}k)$, with adjoined null pairs $v_{j}, w_{j}$ satisfying, as vectors, $v_{i}v_{j} + v_{j}v_{i} = 0$, $w_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}w_{i} = 0$ and $v_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}v_{i} = \delta_{ij}$. Inside $T_{k}$ the subalgebra $B_{k}$ generated by the $2k$ plane generators is $\Cl(k,k) \cong \mathrm{M}_{2^{k}}(\R)$, the twisted ground generators generate a commuting copy $A_{k} \cong \Cl(p,q)$, and multiplication $A_{k} \otimes B_{k} \to T_{k}$ is an isomorphism, $T_{k} \cong \Cl(p,q) \otimes \mathrm{M}_{2^{k}}(\R)$. With $W_{k} = \operatorname{span}\{v_{1}, \ldots, v_{k}\}$ the Chevalley action makes $\Lambda^{\bullet}W_{k}$, of dimension $2^{k}$, an irreducible $B_{k}$-module, the vacuum $1$ annihilated by every $w_{j}$ and cyclic for the $v_{j}$, and each rung doubles it: $\Lambda^{\bullet}W_{k+1} = \Lambda^{\bullet}W_{k} \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}(\R v_{k+1})$, one qubit per rung. The Witt index rises by exactly one per rung, and the Witt index of a real quadratic space is the maximal number of anticommuting mode pairs realisable by vectors. On each complexified floor there is a unique conjugate-linear antiautomorphism $*$ fixing the positive frame generators and negating the negative ones, under which the ladder pairs are mutually adjoint, $v_{j}^{*} = w_{j}$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Def.~2.2, Thm.~3.2, Prop.~4.1, Thms.~4.2, 4.3, Lem.~5.4]{ButlerT3}.
rungs.imported-tower-one-qubit-per-rung.technical:
The transport completes $\Cl(p,q)$ to $\Cl(p+1,q+1)$ by adjoining a hyperbolic pair and iterates, so the $k$-th rung is $T_k = \Cl(p+k,q+k)$, with adjoined null pairs obeying the CAR as vectors: $v_iv_j + v_jv_i = 0$, $w_iw_j + w_jw_i = 0$, $v_iw_j + w_jv_i = \delta_{ij}$. The plane generators give $B_k \cong \Cl(k,k) \cong \Mat_{2^k}(\R)$, the twisted ground generators a commuting copy $A_k \cong \Cl(p,q)$, and $T_k \cong \Cl(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^k}(\R)$.

The Chevalley action makes $\Lambda^\bullet W_k$, with $W_k = \operatorname{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_k\}$, an irreducible $B_k$-module of dimension $2^k$ with vacuum $1$, doubling at each rung: one qubit per rung. The Witt index rises by one per rung and equals the maximal number of anticommuting mode pairs realisable by vectors, and on each complexified floor a unique conjugate-linear antiautomorphism makes the ladder pairs mutually adjoint, $v_j^* = w_j$.
rungs.imported-tower-one-qubit-per-rung.lay: Each completion step adds one pair of directions that behaves exactly like the creation and destruction operators of one fermion. After k steps the algebra splits into the original algebra times a matrix algebra describing k such fermion modes, and the space of states doubles with each step, so each step adds one qubit. The number of independent fermion modes that ordinary directions can carry grows by exactly one per step.

rungs.rung-spinor-module-mixings.formal:
Let $\Cl(2{+}n, 4{+}n)$ be the $n$-th rung of the tower above $\Cl(2,4)$, with new isotropic directions $v_{1}, \ldots, v_{n}$ spanning $R_{n} \cong \C^{n}$ after complexification. The complexification is the odd extension $\Cl(2{+}n, 4{+}n) \otimes \C = \Cl(3{+}n, 4{+}n)$, whose complex unit is the central pseudoscalar $I_{7+2n} = I_{6+2n}e$ ($I_{6+2n}^{2} = -1$ at every rung, so $Q(e) = +1$; \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}); numbers below are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{7+2n}\}$, $I_{13}$ at $n = 3$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Its complexified spinor module is $\Lambda^{\bullet}(W \oplus R_{n}) = \Sp \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}\C^{n}$, of dimension $2^{3+n}$, graded by $(j, k)$ with $j$ the number of new modes and $k$ the number of old pairs occupied, and irreducible; its chirality is the parity of $j + k$. At $n = 2$ this is the five-mode ledger of Hypothesis (S), with the same grading and the same chirality rule.
\item The subgroup of unitaries of $W \oplus R_{n}$ preserving the two summands is $U(3) \times U(n)$, and it acts on the module as $\Lambda^{\bullet}(B \oplus A)$: on $\Lambda^{j}R_{n} \otimes \Lambda^{k}W$ by $\Lambda^{j}(A) \otimes \Lambda^{k}(B)$. At $n = 2$ this is exactly the action Hypothesis (S) prescribes.
\item The Bogoliubov group of the $3 + n$ modes is the compact orthogonal group $O(6{+}2n)$, implemented by $\mathrm{Pin}(6{+}2n)$. At $n = 2$ the connected part is $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$, acting irreducibly on each chirality half; the half of even $j + k$ is the sixteen-dimensional half-spin representation, which under (S) is the generation of Fact \claimref{standard-model.under-s-composites-state-space-spinor}. The number-preserving subgroup of $\mathrm{Spin}(6{+}2n)$ is a double cover of $U(3{+}n)$, acting as $\Lambda^{\bullet} \otimes \det^{-1/2}$; on the determinant-one subgroup this agrees with the action of (2), and it is the determinant-one part that (S) uses (Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-results-t12-used-registration}). At $n = 3$ the group is $\mathrm{Spin}(12)$, and the split-and-number-preserving $U(3) \times U(3)$, of dimension eighteen, acts faithfully on the module, while its action on the cell sector $\Lambda^{1}R_{3} \otimes \Lambda^{1}W = \C^{3} \otimes \C^{3}$ has kernel $K = \{(\lambda 1_{3}, \lambda^{-1}1_{3})\}$ and image the seventeen of Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-ladder-automorphism-group-no-lepton}: the seventeen is the $n = 3$ cell action, exactly as the twelve of $S(U(2) \times U(3))$ is the $n = 2$ cell action of a thirteen-dimensional group on the module. (At $n = 3$ the trace-free subalgebra $\{\tr X + \tr X' = 0\}$ contains $K$'s generator, so the seventeen is the quotient and not that subalgebra, unlike $n = 2$ where $\mathfrak{s}(\uu(2) \oplus \uu(3))$ maps isomorphically onto the cell action. This clause is a relabelling: the cell sector is $\C^{3} \otimes \C^{3}$ with the group Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-ladder-automorphism-group-no-lepton} already has, and nothing about the tower enters.)
\item The dimension counts: $2^{3+n} = 8, 16, 32, 64$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, 3$; $\dim \mathfrak{so}(6{+}2n) = 15, 28, 45, 66$; $\dim(\uu(3) \oplus \uu(n)) = 9, 10, 13, 18$.
\end{enumerate}
rungs.rung-spinor-module-mixings.technical:
For the $n$-th rung $\Cl(2+n,4+n)$ above $\Cl(2,4)$, with new isotropic directions spanning $R_n \cong \C^n$ after complexification, the complexified spinor module is $\Lambda^\bullet(W \oplus R_n) = \Sp \otimes \Lambda^\bullet\C^n$, irreducible of dimension $2^{3+n}$, bigraded by the number $j$ of new modes and $k$ of old pairs occupied, with chirality the parity of $j + k$. The summand-preserving unitaries $U(3) \times U(n)$ act on $\Lambda^j R_n \otimes \Lambda^k W$ by $\Lambda^j(A) \otimes \Lambda^k(B)$; at $n = 2$ the module, grading, chirality and action are those of Hypothesis (S).

The Bogoliubov group of the $3+n$ modes is $O(6+2n)$, implemented by $\Pin(6+2n)$; at $n = 2$ its connected part $\Spin(10)$ acts irreducibly on each chirality half, the even half being the sixteen-dimensional half-spin representation. The number-preserving subgroup of $\Spin(6+2n)$ double covers $U(3+n)$, acting as $\Lambda^\bullet \otimes \det^{-1/2}$, which agrees with the split action on the determinant-one part. At $n = 3$, $U(3) \times U(3)$ acts faithfully on the module, while on the cell sector $\C^3 \otimes \C^3$ it has kernel $K = \{(\lambda 1_3, \lambda^{-1} 1_3)\}$ and image the seventeen-dimensional group of the ladder. The dimensions are $2^{3+n} = 8, 16, 32, 64$, $\dim \mathfrak{so}(6+2n) = 15, 28, 45, 66$ and $\dim(\uu(3) \oplus \uu(n)) = 9, 10, 13, 18$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, 3$.
rungs.rung-spinor-module-mixings.lay: Each rung of the tower above the conformal algebra adds new fermionic modes to the three already present, and the full state space is built by filling any combination of them, doubling in size with every new mode. The symmetries that keep old and new modes separate act on this space in a definite way, and with two new modes they match the structure the series' Hypothesis (S) prescribes; Spin(10) then acts on a sixteen-state half, which under that hypothesis is one generation. With three new modes the symmetry acting on the mixed sector is the seventeen-dimensional group found earlier, which the result records as a relabelling.

proofs.main: (1) By Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-tower-one-qubit-per-rung}, $T_{n} \cong \Cl(2,4) \otimes \mathrm{M}_{2^{n}}(\R)$, and after complexification $\Cl(2,4) \otimes \C \cong \mathrm{M}_{8}(\C)$ acting irreducibly on $\Sp = \Lambda^{\bullet}W$ (Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-spinor-identification-witt-data-line}) while $B_{n} \otimes \C \cong \mathrm{M}_{2^{n}}(\C)$ acts irreducibly on $\Lambda^{\bullet}W_{n} \otimes \C = \Lambda^{\bullet}R_{n}$ (Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-tower-one-qubit-per-rung}); the tensor product $\mathrm{M}_{8} \otimes \mathrm{M}_{2^{n}} = \mathrm{M}_{8 \cdot 2^{n}}$ acts irreducibly on $\Sp \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}R_{n}$, which is the whole endomorphism algebra of that space, so this is the spinor module of $T_{n} \otimes \C$, of dimension $2^{3+n}$. The step from the twisted presentation to the mode grading: the tensor decomposition $A_{n} \otimes B_{n}$ of Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-tower-one-qubit-per-rung} presents $T_{n}$ through the twisted ground generators, which are not vectors of $\R^{2+n,4+n}$; but $T_{n} \otimes \C$ is also generated by the $6 + 2n$ untwisted vectors, so it is the complex Clifford algebra on $6 + 2n$ generators (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification}), $\mathrm{M}_{2^{3+n}}(\C)$, whose irreducible module is unique up to isomorphism and is the Fock module of any $3 + n$ anticommuting mode pairs (Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-fock-representation-bogoliubov-group}); the pairs of $W$ with its dual and the untwisted $(v_{j}, w_{j})$ are such a set, and their Fock module is $\Lambda^{\bullet}(W \oplus R_{n})$ by the direct-sum formula for exterior algebras \cite[App.~B.2]{FultonHarris1991}, with the grading by occupied modes the bigrading $\Lambda^{j}R_{n} \otimes \Lambda^{k}W$. The irreducibility established through $A_{n} \otimes B_{n}$ transfers to this presentation because the module is the same up to isomorphism. The chirality of a Fock module is its parity grading (Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-fock-representation-bogoliubov-group}), here $(-1)^{j+k}$. At $n = 2$, $R_{2} = \C^{2}$ and the description is (S)'s. (2) A unitary of $W \oplus R_{n}$ preserving the summands is $B \oplus A$, and the induced action on the exterior algebra is $\Lambda^{\bullet}(B \oplus A) = \Lambda^{\bullet}(B) \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}(A)$ on $\Lambda^{\bullet}W \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}R_{n}$, degree by degree. (3) is Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-fock-representation-bogoliubov-group} with $E = W \oplus R_{n}$, $\dim E = 3 + n$, the Hermitian structure being the one under which $v_{j}^{*} = w_{j}$ (Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-tower-one-qubit-per-rung}); the double cover and the $\det^{-1/2}$ twist are the "determinant phase" of Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-fock-representation-bogoliubov-group}, absent on the determinant-one subgroup. The $n = 3$ clause: $\uu(3) \oplus \uu(3)$ has dimension $18$; $K$'s generator $(I_{13}1_{3}, -I_{13}1_{3})$, with $1_{3}$ the identity of $\C^{3}$ and $I_{13}$ the complex unit of $\Cl(5,7) \otimes \C = \Cl(6,7)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), acts on $\Lambda^{j}R_{3} \otimes \Lambda^{k}W$ by $I_{13}(j - k)$, zero exactly on the cells $j = k = 1$ and nonzero on the module, so the action on the module is faithful and the action on the cells has kernel $K$; the quotient, of dimension $17$, is the seventeen of Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-ladder-automorphism-group-no-lepton}; and the trace-free subalgebra, which contains the kernel since $\tr(I_{13}1_{3}) + \tr(-I_{13}1_{3}) = 0$, acts on the cells with rank $16$ only. The script confirms the ranks $17$ and $16$ at $n = 3$ against $12$ and $12$ at $n = 2$, and the eigenvalue $j - k$. (4) is arithmetic, script-checked.

scrambling.pair-mode-qubit-one-object.formal: The tower's ladder pair $(v_i, w_i)$, the singularity paper's ``fermionic mode'', and the ``one ladder pair per point of the exceptional set'' (the degeneration there has corank exactly one at every point, Theorem \claimref{sheaf.schwarzschild-degeneration-boundary-tame}(2), so the completion adds one ladder pair per point) are the same object: one creation and one annihilation operator, a two-dimensional state space, one qubit, maximal entropy $\ln 2$ nats. In particular $\Cl(2,4)$ carries exactly two such pairs, its Witt index, and the count of pairs is the count of modes: no factor of two enters between the tower and this paper's count.
scrambling.pair-mode-qubit-one-object.technical:
The tower's ladder pair $(v_i, w_i)$, the singularity analysis's fermionic mode, and the one ladder pair per point of the exceptional set (the singular boundary degenerates with corank exactly one at every point) are one object: one creation and one annihilation operator, a two-dimensional state space $\{\ket{0}, v_i\ket{0}\}$, one qubit, of maximal entropy $\ln 2$ nats.

In particular $\Cl(2,4)$ carries exactly two such pairs, its Witt index, and the count of pairs is the count of modes, with no factor of two between the tower's count and the entropy count.
scrambling.pair-mode-qubit-one-object.lay: Three things in the series that sound different, a pair of null directions in the tower, a fermionic mode in the singularity analysis and a unit of quantum capacity, are the same thing. Each is one fermion mode with two states, empty or filled, which is one qubit and can hold at most $\ln 2$ nats of entropy. The conformal algebra has room for exactly two of them, and counting pairs or counting modes gives the same number.
scrambling.pair-mode-qubit-one-object.typing_note: All three uses are the tower results the proof cites and are kept.

proofs.main: The tower's relations \cite[Prop.~4.1]{ButlerT3} (\claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}) are the CAR of $k$ modes with $v_i$ the creation and $w_i$ the annihilation operator of mode $i$, each mode's algebra $\Mat_2$ with the two-dimensional Fock space $\{|0\rangle, v_i|0\rangle\}$, one qubit per rung \cite[Thm.~4.2]{ButlerT3} (\claimref{tower.fock-module-one-qubit-per-rung}); the singularity paper's per-mode capacity $\ln 2$ is the maximal entropy of that two-state system; the corank statement counts these pairs. The script realises two pairs in $\Cl(2,4)$ as $v_i = \tfrac12(e_a + e_b)$, $w_i = \tfrac12(e_a - e_b)$ on two orthogonal hyperbolic planes and checks all ten anticommutation relations exactly, the CAR of a Witt basis (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-basis-car}); that no third pair exists is the capacity theorem \cite[Thm.~4.3]{ButlerT3} (\claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity}). The exceptional set's one ladder pair per point is the corank-one degeneration of Theorem \claimref{sheaf.schwarzschild-degeneration-boundary-tame}(2): at every point of the blown-up singular boundary exactly one direction degenerates, so its completion adds exactly one hyperbolic plane, one ladder pair.

standard-model.imported-tower-commuting-.formal: The transport principle completes $\Cl(p,q)$ to $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ by adjoining one hyperbolic pair, and iterates: the $k$-th rung is $T_{k} = \Cl(p{+}k, q{+}k)$ with adjoined null pairs $v_{j}, w_{j}$ satisfying $v_{i}v_{j} + v_{j}v_{i} = 0$, $w_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}w_{i} = 0$, $v_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}v_{i} = \delta_{ij}$. Inside $T_{k}$ the subalgebra $B_{k}$ generated by the $2k$ plane generators is $\Cl(k,k) \cong \mathrm{M}_{2^{k}}(\R)$, the twisted ground generators $x\,\omega_{1}\cdots\omega_{k}$ generate a commuting copy $A_{k} \cong \Cl(p,q)$, and multiplication $A_{k} \otimes B_{k} \to T_{k}$ is an isomorphism. The Chevalley action makes $\Lambda^{\bullet}\operatorname{span}(v_{1}, \ldots, v_{k})$ an irreducible $B_{k}$-module, one qubit per rung. On each complexified floor there is a conjugate-linear antiautomorphism $*$ under which the ladder pairs are mutually adjoint, $v_{j}^{*} = w_{j}$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thms.~3.2, 4.2]{ButlerT3}; proved there.
standard-model.imported-tower-commuting-.technical:
The transport completes $\Cl(p,q)$ to $\Cl(p+1,q+1)$ by adjoining one hyperbolic pair, and iterates: the $k$-th rung is $T_k = \Cl(p+k,q+k)$, with adjoined null pairs satisfying $v_iv_j + v_jv_i = 0$, $w_iw_j + w_jw_i = 0$, $v_iw_j + w_jv_i = \delta_{ij}$. Inside $T_k$ the plane generators give $B_k \cong \Cl(k,k) \cong \Mat_{2^k}(\R)$, the twisted ground generators $x\,\omega_1 \cdots \omega_k$ give a commuting copy $A_k \cong \Cl(p,q)$, and multiplication $A_k \otimes B_k \to T_k$ is an isomorphism.

The Chevalley action makes $\Lambda^\bullet \operatorname{span}(v_1, \ldots, v_k)$ an irreducible $B_k$-module, one qubit per rung, and on each complexified floor a conjugate-linear antiautomorphism makes the ladder pairs mutually adjoint, $v_j^* = w_j$.
standard-model.imported-tower-commuting-.lay: Each completion step adds a pair of directions that acts like the creation and destruction operators of one fermion. After k steps the algebra is the original one alongside an independent matrix algebra for the k fermion modes, the two commuting with each other. The fermion modes act on a state space that doubles with every step, one qubit per step.

proofs.main:
The transport principle completes $\Cl(p,q)$ to $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ by adjoining one hyperbolic pair, and iterates: the $k$-th rung is $T_{k} = \Cl(p{+}k, q{+}k)$ with adjoined null pairs $v_{j}, w_{j}$ satisfying $v_{i}v_{j} + v_{j}v_{i} = 0$, $w_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}w_{i} = 0$, $v_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}v_{i} = \delta_{ij}$. Inside $T_{k}$ the subalgebra $B_{k}$ generated by the $2k$ plane generators is $\Cl(k,k) \cong \mathrm{M}_{2^{k}}(\R)$, the twisted ground generators $x\,\omega_{1}\cdots\omega_{k}$ generate a commuting copy $A_{k} \cong \Cl(p,q)$, and multiplication $A_{k} \otimes B_{k} \to T_{k}$ is an isomorphism. The Chevalley action makes $\Lambda^{\bullet}\operatorname{span}(v_{1}, \ldots, v_{k})$ an irreducible $B_{k}$-module, one qubit per rung. On each complexified floor there is a conjugate-linear antiautomorphism $*$ under which the ladder pairs are mutually adjoint, $v_{j}^{*} = w_{j}$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thms.~3.2, 4.2]{ButlerT3} (\claimref{tower.fock-module-one-qubit-per-rung}, \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}); proved there.

synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tow.formal:
Let $B_{k} = \Cl(k,k)$ be the algebra of $k$ ladder pairs $v_{i}, w_{i}$ (Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}) and $F_{k} = \Lambda^{\bullet}W_{k}$ its Fock module, of dimension $2^{k}$, with the basis of states $v_{S}$, $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.fock-module-one-qubit-per-rung}). Call a family $(a_{i}, b_{i})_{i \le m}$ of elements of a real associative algebra with unit a \emph{CAR family} if $a_{i}a_{j} + a_{j}a_{i} = 0$, $b_{i}b_{j} + b_{j}b_{i} = 0$ and $a_{i}b_{j} + b_{j}a_{i} = \delta_{ij}$. The exponential reading of Observation \claimref{standard-model.why-large} (each level's objects are the fermionic pairs of the level above, with counts $3$, $8$, $256$, $2^{256}$) has the following precise forms, on the split tower $B_{0} = \R \subset B_{1} \subset B_{2} \subset \cdots$, with the base level taken as $B_{3} = \Cl(3,3)$, three real pairs. The base three of the stored reading is the complex capacity of the space of signature $(2,4)$, whose real capacity is two (Theorem \claimref{one-relation.two-capacities-three-consequences}); clauses (i), (iii) and (iv) use only dimensions and hold for the complexified floors with complex dimensions, and from a base of two real pairs the recursion of (i) would read $2, 4, 16, 65536$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Under the rule "states become creators" the counts hold.)} Let the level above $B_{k}$ be the Clifford algebra of $F_{k} \oplus F_{k}^{*}$ with the form $Q(x + \phi) = \phi(x)$: the states become creators and as many annihilators are adjoined. The states $V_{S} = v_{S}$ and the dual basis $W_{S}$ are a CAR family of $2^{k}$ vectors, so this algebra is $B_{2^{k}}$ and its Fock module is $\Lambda^{\bullet}F_{k}$, of dimension $2^{2^{k}}$. Iterating from $c_{0} = 3$ gives $c_{n+1} = 2^{c_{n}}$: $3$, $8$, $256$, $2^{256}$. Under this rule $2^{256}$ is the number of ladder pairs of the third level above the base, equal to the number of states of the $256$ pairs of the second.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The step of (i) is not a step of the ascent.)} One step of the transport ascent adjoins one hyperbolic plane and raises the number of pairs of a CAR family of vectors by exactly one (Theorem \claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity}); $2^{k} = k + 1$ only for $k \in \{0, 1\}$. From three pairs one ascent gives $B_{4}$: four pairs and a module of dimension $16$, against the eight pairs and $256$ states of (i). The same holds for the stored complex base: the complex capacity also rises by one per ascent, so three complex pairs become four (Theorem \claimref{one-relation.two-capacities-three-consequences}). The level above of (i) is reached from $B_{k}$ by $2^{k} - k$ ascents.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Inside a level the counts fail for every kind of element.)} A CAR family of $m$ pairs in a real associative algebra $A$ with unit, of finite dimension, generates a copy of $\Mat_{2^{m}}(\R)$ containing the unit, so $4^{m} \le \dim A$. Hence $B_{j}$ holds no CAR family of more than $j$ pairs, of vectors or of any other elements, and a floor $\Cl(p + j, q + j)$ holds none of more than $j + (p+q)/2$ pairs; this last is a bound, equal to the stored complex capacity, not a count, and on a floor that is not split families of elements that are not vectors can exceed the Witt index (in $\Cl(2,0)$, of Witt index zero, $a = \tfrac12(e_{1} + e_{1}e_{2})$, $b = \tfrac12(e_{1} - e_{1}e_{2})$ is a CAR pair). The $2^{k}$ states of a level are therefore the pairs of a CAR family in $B_{j}$ only for $j \ge 2^{k}$: the level above of (i) is the floor $2^{k}$, by any identification of a basis of $F_{k}$ with its ladder vectors, and the floors strictly between consecutive levels of the reading ($4$ floors between three pairs and eight, $247$ between eight and $256$) are floors of the same tower that the reading passes over. The construction (i) names the floors $c_{n}$; no stored result on the tower selects them (argued, from a reading of the stored tower results and not from an audit of the tower region).
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The level above does not inherit the ladder through the second-quantised lift.)} For an endomorphism $X$ of $F_{k}$ with matrix $X_{TS}$ in the states, put $L(X) = \sum_{T,S} X_{TS}V_{T}W_{S}$ in the level above (the lift that Theorem \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation} names for the field algebra). Then $[L(X), L(Y)] = L([X, Y])$, and $L(X)$ acts on $\Lambda^{\bullet}F_{k}$ as the derivation extending $X$. The lifted ladder is not a CAR family: $L(v_{1})L(w_{1}) + L(w_{1})L(v_{1})$ annihilates the vacuum of the level above, so it is not $1$, for every $k \ge 1$, and $L(v_{1})^{2} \neq 0$ for every $k \ge 2$. The tower's own inclusions $B_{j} \subset B_{j+1}$ keep every relation of the ladder. This clause concerns the lift $L$ only: whether $F_{k}$ carries other structure that makes its states vectors of a next level, such as an invariant bilinear form, is a separate question, not treated here, and such a rule gives other counts than (i) (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.invariant-forms-on-the-fock-module-and-the-pair-counts-of-a-next-level}(v)).
\item[(v)] \emph{(Where the horizon count falls, as a comparison of sizes only.)} The horizon count is $|J| = \pi N^{2}/\ln 2 \approx 4.8 \times 10^{122}$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.de-sitter-mode-count}); the store quotes $2^{407} < |J| < 2^{408}$ (the check of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.trichotomy-what-kind-number} and the technical level of the stored entry on largeness; quoted, not recomputed here). Given that bracket, $c_{3} = 2^{256} < |J| < 2^{2^{256}} = c_{4}$, as for every number whose base-two logarithm lies between $256$ and $2^{256}$; and a module of at least $|J|$ states first occurs at the floor $408$. The comparison is of sizes only: the stored count is of registered units averaging two arrays, not of ladder pairs or rungs, and no single ladder pair qualifies as a unit (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.the-residue-requires-two-arrays-per-unit-on-average-and-fixes-no-grouping}); the trichotomy's "one qubit per rung" is a statement of units.
\end{enumerate}
So the reading, under the rule of (i), is a true statement about iterating $k \mapsto \dim F_{k}$ and a false one about a step of the ascent: its levels are the floors $3$, $8$, $256$ of the one tower, reached by $2^{k} - k$ ascents each. The rule of (i) is one of at least two counting rules with a claim to the stored wording (a rule through an invariant form of the module gives other counts, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.invariant-forms-on-the-fock-module-and-the-pair-counts-of-a-next-level}(v)), and nothing stored selects one of them (argued, on the same reading of the stored tower results). As a reading, not a theorem: on the proved tower the number of pairs at the floor $j$ is $j$ and only the number of states, $2^{j}$, grows exponentially, so a large number of pairs is not singled out by the tower; the stored entry on largeness says the same in its technical level.
synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tow.technical:
The exponential reading of the tower says that the objects of each level are the fermionic pairs of the level above, with counts 3, 8, 256, $2^{256}$. Made precise on the split tower $\Cl(k,k)$ under the rule that the $2^{k}$ states of $k$ ladder pairs become the creators of a new set of pairs, with as many annihilators adjoined, it is the second quantisation of the Fock module, and as arithmetic it holds exactly: three pairs have eight states, eight pairs have 256, and $2^{256}$ is the number of pairs of the next level. That step is not a step of the tower's ascent: one ascent from three pairs gives four pairs and sixteen states (for three real pairs and for the stored complex count on signature $(2,4)$ alike). Inside the algebra of $j$ pairs no family of more than $j$ anticommuting pairs exists, whether of vectors or of general elements, by a dimension count valid for any real associative algebra; on floors that are not split this is only a bound. And the second-quantised lift of a level's ladder operators to the level above preserves commutators but not the anticommutation relations (other structure on the module, such as an invariant form, is not treated and gives other counts).

The levels of the reading are therefore the floors 3, 8, 256, $2^{256}$ of the proved tower, with 4 and then 247 floors passed over. That nothing stored selects those floors, or this rule over another, is argued from a reading of the stored tower results, not from an audit. Given the stored bracket for the horizon count, $2^{407} < |J| < 2^{408}$, the count lies between the third and fourth levels of the reading, as does any number with base-two logarithm between 256 and $2^{256}$; this compares sizes only, since the stored count is of registered units and not of ladder pairs. The checks are exact: ranks of left ideals in $\Cl(3,3)$ and $\Cl(4,4)$, the anticommutation relations of eight state-indexed pairs in $\Cl(8,8)$ and its rank-one vacuum idempotent, non-vector families filling $\Cl(2,2)$ and $\Cl(3,3)$, a non-vector pair in $\Cl(2,0)$, and the lift for two and three pairs.
synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tow.lay: One unproved reading of the programme's tower says each level is built from the level below by an exponential step, giving the counts 3, 8, 256 and then a number with 77 digits, so that huge numbers come for free. This result makes that reading exact and tests it. Under the rule "take every state of the level below as a new basic mode", the counts are right: it is a standard construction, but it is not a step of the kind the tower's theorems describe. The proved step adds one mode at a time, so three modes become four, not eight, and no cleverer choice of modes inside a level can do better. The exponential levels are floors number 3, 8 and 256 of the ordinary tower. On our reading of the stored results, which is an argument and not a complete audit, nothing in the theory picks those floors out, and this rule is only one of at least two that fit the original wording. The test is done for three real modes; the three of the original reading is a count over complex numbers on a space whose real count is two, and for it too one step gives four. So, given the tower as proved, only the number of states grows exponentially; the number of modes grows one at a time.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i).} For $x, y \in F_{k}$ and $\phi, \psi \in F_{k}^{*}$ the form $Q(x + \phi) = \phi(x)$ gives $x^{2} = 0$, $\phi^{2} = 0$ and $x\phi + \phi x = Q(x + \phi) - Q(x) - Q(\phi) = \phi(x)$ in the Clifford algebra, so the basis $V_{S}$ of $F_{k}$ and the dual basis $W_{S}$ are a CAR family of $2^{k}$ vectors; they span $2^{k}$ orthogonal hyperbolic planes, so the algebra is $\Cl(2^{k}, 2^{k}) = B_{2^{k}}$ and by Theorem \claimref{tower.fock-module-one-qubit-per-rung} its Fock module is the exterior algebra of the span of the $V_{S}$, which is $\Lambda^{\bullet}F_{k}$, of dimension $2^{2^{k}}$. The recursion $c_{n+1} = 2^{c_{n}}$ from $c_{0} = 3$ is $3, 2^{3} = 8, 2^{8} = 256, 2^{256}$. The script computes the dimension $8$ as the rank of the left ideal $B_{3}P$ on the vacuum idempotent $P = \prod_{j}w_{j}v_{j}$, the relations of the eight state-indexed pairs in $\Cl(8,8)$, and the dimension $256$ twice: the vacuum idempotent of $\Cl(8,8)$ has scalar part $2^{-8}$, the normalised trace of an idempotent of rank one in $\Mat_{256}(\R)$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} with $p = q = 0$), so its left ideal has dimension $4^{8} \cdot 2^{-8} = 256$; and on the exterior algebra of eight letters the contractions have a common kernel of dimension one and the creation monomials reach $256$ states.

\emph{(ii).} Theorem \claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity}: along the tower the maximal number of pairs of a CAR family of vectors is the Witt index, which rises by exactly one per rung. For $k \ge 2$, $2^{k} > k + 1$ (induction: $2^{k+1} = 2 \cdot 2^{k} > 2k + 2 > k + 2$), and $2^{0} = 1$, $2^{1} = 2$. From $B_{3}$ the ascent gives $B_{4}$, with four pairs and a module of dimension $2^{4} = 16$ (computed as a rank). For the complex base, Theorem \claimref{one-relation.two-capacities-three-consequences} gives complex capacity $\lfloor (p+q)/2 \rfloor$, three for $(2,4)$ and rising by one per ascent. The floor $2^{k}$ is $2^{k} - k$ ascents above the floor $k$.

\emph{(iii).} Let $(a_{i}, b_{i})_{i \le m}$ be a CAR family in $A$ and put $x_{i} = a_{i} + b_{i}$, $y_{i} = a_{i} - b_{i}$. From $a_{i}^{2} = b_{i}^{2} = 0$ and the relations, $x_{i}^{2} = 1$, $y_{i}^{2} = -1$, and the $2m$ elements anticommute pairwise: $x_{i}y_{j} + y_{j}x_{i} = -(a_{i}b_{j} + b_{j}a_{i}) + (b_{i}a_{j} + a_{j}b_{i}) = 0$, and $x_{i}x_{j} + x_{j}x_{i} = 2\delta_{ij} = -(y_{i}y_{j} + y_{j}y_{i})$. By the universal property (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.existence-uniqueness}) there is a homomorphism $\Cl(m,m) \to A$ sending the generators to the $x_{i}, y_{i}$ and $1$ to $1$. $\Cl(m,m) \cong \Mat_{2^{m}}(\R)$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}) is simple (Proposition \claimref{tower.matrix-amplification-structural-properties}), and the kernel is a two-sided ideal not containing $1$, so the map is injective and $4^{m} = \dim\Cl(m,m) \le \dim A$. With $\dim B_{j} = 4^{j}$ this gives $m \le j$, and with $\dim\Cl(p + j, q + j) = 2^{p+q}4^{j}$ it gives $m \le j + (p+q)/2$. Since $2^{k} > k$ for all $k \ge 0$, the $2^{k}$ states of the level $B_{k}$ are not the pairs of a CAR family in $B_{j}$ for any $j < 2^{k}$, and for $j = 2^{k}$ the ladder vectors of $B_{2^{k}}$ are such a family, identified with the states by any bijection of bases. The floors strictly between the levels $c_{n}$ and $c_{n+1}$ number $c_{n+1} - c_{n} - 1$: $8 - 3 - 1 = 4$ and $256 - 8 - 1 = 247$. The stored results on the tower (the Fock module, the capacity theorem, the commuting copies, the rigidity and limit theorems, the iteration theorem) are statements for every floor $j$ or for the limit; none distinguishes a floor of the form $2^{k}$; this is a reading of those statements, not an audit of the tower region, and the selection sentence is argued on it. The bound $j + (p+q)/2$ is the complex capacity of Theorem \claimref{one-relation.two-capacities-three-consequences} when $p + q$ is even; it need not be attained by real families. On a floor that is not split a family of elements that are not vectors can exceed the Witt index: in $\Cl(2,0)$, with $e_{1}^{2} = e_{2}^{2} = 1$ and $(e_{1}e_{2})^{2} = -1$, the elements $a = \tfrac12(e_{1} + e_{1}e_{2})$ and $b = \tfrac12(e_{1} - e_{1}e_{2})$ have $a^{2} = b^{2} = 0$ and $ab + ba = 1$ (computed), while the Witt index is zero. The script checks the dimension count on families that are not vectors: the ladder of $B_{2}$ and of $B_{3}$ conjugated by the unit $1 + v_{1}e_{2}f_{2}$ (the trivector is nilpotent) is a CAR family whose ordered monomials have rank $16$ and $64$, the whole algebra.

\emph{(iv).} Using $W_{S}V_{T'} = \delta_{ST'} - V_{T'}W_{S}$,
\[
V_{T}W_{S}V_{T'}W_{S'} = \delta_{ST'}V_{T}W_{S'} - V_{T}V_{T'}W_{S}W_{S'} ,
\]
and the last term is symmetric under exchange of the two factors $(T, S) \leftrightarrow (T', S')$ (two sign changes), so $[V_{T}W_{S}, V_{T'}W_{S'}] = \delta_{ST'}V_{T}W_{S'} - \delta_{S'T}V_{T'}W_{S}$ and $[L(X), L(Y)] = L([X, Y])$ by linearity. Each $W_{S}$ annihilates the vacuum $\Omega$ of $\Lambda^{\bullet}F_{k}$, so $L(X)\Omega = 0$; on a state $x = \sum_{S}x_{S}V_{S}\Omega$ of one letter $L(X)x = Xx$; and $[L(X), V_{T}] = \sum_{T'}X_{T'T}V_{T'}$, so $L(X)$ is the derivation of the exterior algebra extending $X$ (the map that Theorem \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation} names $d\Gamma$ for the field algebra). Hence $\bigl(L(v_{1})L(w_{1}) + L(w_{1})L(v_{1})\bigr)\Omega = 0 \neq \Omega$. For $k \ge 2$ take the states $x = v_{\emptyset}$ and $y = v_{\{2\}}$: since $v_{1}^{2} = 0$ on $F_{k}$, $L(v_{1})^{2}(x \wedge y) = 2\,v_{1}x \wedge v_{1}y = 2\,v_{\{1\}} \wedge v_{\{1,2\}} \neq 0$, and the module is faithful. The script computes the commutator of the lifted pair, the nonzero square ($16$ and $96$ blade terms) and two failing anticommutators in $\Cl(4,4)$ and $\Cl(8,8)$. That the inclusions $B_{j} \subset B_{j+1}$ keep the relations is Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}.

\emph{(v).} $|J| = \pi N^{2}/\ln 2$ is Theorem \claimref{synthesis.de-sitter-mode-count}(ii) in the capacity convention. The bracket $2^{407} < |J| < 2^{408}$ is quoted: the text of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.trichotomy-what-kind-number} says "about $407$" for the base-two logarithm, its check asserts that the integer part of the logarithm is $407$ for counts between $4.75$ and $4.85 \times 10^{122}$, and the technical level of the stored entry on largeness states the bracket. Given it, $256 < 407$ and $408 < 2^{256}$ give $2^{256} < 2^{407} < |J| < 2^{408} < 2^{2^{256}}$; the same holds for any number with base-two logarithm between $256$ and $2^{256}$. On the proved tower the module of the floor $j$ has $2^{j}$ states, at least $|J|$ exactly when $j \ge 408$. That the count is of registered units averaging two arrays, with no single ladder pair qualifying, is Theorem \claimref{synthesis.the-residue-requires-two-arrays-per-unit-on-average-and-fixes-no-grouping}; no identification of units with pairs is made.

synthesis.invariant-forms-on-the-fock-mo.formal:
\emph{Setting.} Let $B_{k} = \Cl(k,k)$, $k \ge 1$, be the algebra of $k$ rungs with its null pairs $v_{j}, w_{j}$ ($j = 1, \ldots, k$), $v_{i}v_{j} + v_{j}v_{i} = 0$, $w_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}w_{i} = 0$, $v_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}v_{i} = \delta_{ij}$, over a field of characteristic zero (the rationals in the checks). Write $v_{S} = v_{s_{1}}\cdots v_{s_{r}}$ for a subset $S = \{s_{1} < \cdots < s_{r}\}$ of the rungs, $S^{c}$ for its complement, $p_{k} = \prod_{j} w_{j}v_{j}$ for the vacuum idempotent and $\Omega_{k} = v_{1}v_{2}\cdots v_{k}$. The left ideal $F_{k} = B_{k}p_{k}$ has the basis $v_{S}p_{k}$ and is the Fock module of Theorem \claimref{tower.fock-module-one-qubit-per-rung}, of dimension $2^{k}$, the minimal left ideal on the vacuum idempotent of Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.fock-representation} with the two null families exchanged. Let $\tau_{+}$ be the reverse and $\tau_{-}$ the reverse composed with the grade involution, so that $\tau_{\epsilon}(a) = \epsilon a$ for every vector $a$, $\epsilon = \pm 1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The two forms.)} For $\psi, \phi \in F_{k}$ the product $\tau_{\epsilon}(\psi)\phi$ is a multiple of $\Omega_{k}$, and
\[
\tau_{\epsilon}(\psi)\,\phi \;=\; \beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, \phi)\,\Omega_{k}
\]
defines a nondegenerate bilinear form $\beta_{\epsilon}$ on $F_{k}$ with $\beta_{\epsilon}(a\psi, \phi) = \epsilon\,\beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, a\phi)$ for every vector $a$ of $B_{k}$; on the basis, $\beta_{\epsilon}(v_{S}p_{k}, v_{T}p_{k}) = \pm 1$ if $T = S^{c}$ and $0$ otherwise. For $\epsilon = +1$ this restates Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.chevalley-pairing}: $\beta_{+}$ is its pairing up to a factor. Added here: $\beta_{-}(\psi, \phi) = \beta_{+}(\alpha\psi, \phi)$ up to a factor, with $\alpha$ the grade involution on the module (the sign $(-1)^{|S|}$ on $v_{S}p_{k}$), and uniqueness: every bilinear form on $F_{k}$ with the adjoint property for $\epsilon$ is a multiple of $\beta_{\epsilon}$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Symmetry.)} $\beta_{\epsilon}(\phi, \psi) = s_{\epsilon}(k)\,\beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, \phi)$ with $s_{\epsilon}(k) = \epsilon^{k}(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$ (for $\epsilon = +1$ the stored law of Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.chevalley-pairing}(ii)): $\beta_{+}$ is symmetric for $k \equiv 0, 1$ and antisymmetric for $k \equiv 2, 3 \pmod 4$; $\beta_{-}$ is symmetric for $k \equiv 0, 3$ and antisymmetric for $k \equiv 1, 2 \pmod 4$. So $F_{k}$ carries a symmetric form of this kind exactly when $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and an antisymmetric one exactly when $k \not\equiv 0 \pmod 4$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Neutral, and the count of pairs.)} A symmetric $\beta_{\epsilon}$ is the orthogonal sum of the $2^{k-1}$ hyperbolic planes spanned by $v_{S}p_{k}$ and $v_{S^{c}}p_{k}$: the quadratic space $(F_{k}, \beta_{\epsilon})$ is hyperbolic over any field of characteristic not two, of signature $(2^{k-1}, 2^{k-1})$ over an ordered field, with Witt index $2^{k-1}$. By Theorem \claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity} its Clifford algebra carries exactly $2^{k-1}$ fermionic mode pairs realised by vectors, and no nondegenerate quadratic form on the $2^{k}$-dimensional space $F_{k}$ gives more. An antisymmetric $\beta_{\epsilon}$ is a symplectic form with the $2^{k-1}$ canonically conjugate pairs $(v_{S}p_{k}, \pm v_{S^{c}}p_{k})$. For odd $k$ the even and odd parity halves of $F_{k}$ are each totally null and are paired with each other; for even $k$ each half is nondegenerate (the stored grade pairing, Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.chevalley-pairing}(i), which holds for both forms).
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Three pairs, and two.)} At $k = 3$: $\beta_{+}$ is antisymmetric, $\beta_{-}$ is symmetric of signature $(4, 4)$, and the two four-dimensional parity halves are complementary totally null subspaces. So under the invariant symmetric form the eight states of three pairs are the vectors of four pairs. This four is a Witt index. The four of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tower-is-the-iterated-fock-functor-not-the-ascent}(ii) is a different object, the pair count of the tower's next floor $B_{4}$ after one ascent; the two agree as numbers: an equality of counts, $2^{k-1} = k + 1$, which holds for $k = 3$ and for no other $k \ge 1$, and which is not an identification of the two constructions. $(F_{3}, \beta_{-})$ and the vector space of $B_{4}$ are isometric, as any two hyperbolic spaces of dimension eight are, but no isometry is compatible with the action of $B_{3}$: the bivectors of $B_{3}$ annihilate no nonzero vector of $F_{3}$, while in their commutator action on the vector space of $B_{4}$ they annihilate the plane of $v_{4}, w_{4}$; and from four the rule of (v) gives eight, not five. At $k = 2$ both forms are antisymmetric, so the four states carry no invariant quadratic form of this kind.
\item[(v)] \emph{(A second rule for a next level.)} Call the $2^{k}$ basis states of $F_{k}$ the objects of a level with $k$ pairs. The rule in which the objects become creators and as many annihilators are adjoined is Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tower-is-the-iterated-fock-functor-not-the-ascent}(i), with the stored counts $3, 8, 256, 2^{256}$; it is not repeated here. Second rule: the objects, with an invariant symmetric form ($\beta_{-}$ at $k = 3$, the only one there; either form from $k = 4$ on, where both are symmetric), are the generating vectors of the next level, which is then the floor $B_{2^{k-1}}$ of the tower. From three the pair counts run $3, 4, 8, 128, 2^{127}$ (every term after the first is divisible by four, so a symmetric form exists at each step), with state counts $8, 16, 256, 2^{128}$; from two this rule does not start. It does not reproduce the stored counts: $8$ and $256$ recur in it only as state counts of its first and third levels, and its next number is $2^{128} \approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}$ against $2^{256}$. A judgement, not a result: the second rule is another reading of the stored phrase, objects of a level as the fermionic pairs of the next. Given the bracket $2^{407} < |J| < 2^{408}$ of the horizon count quoted in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tower-is-the-iterated-fock-functor-not-the-ascent}(v), and with its rider that the comparison is of sizes only (the stored count is of registered units, not of ladder pairs), $|J|$ lies between the consecutive terms $2^{127}$ and $2^{2^{127} - 1}$ of the second rule, as it lies between consecutive terms of the first. Argued, from a search of the stored tower results and not from an audit of a full cone: no stored result selects one rule. The only growth the series proves is one pair per rung, which neither rule is.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.invariant-forms-on-the-fock-mo.technical:
Let $B_{k} = \Cl(k,k)$ be the algebra of $k$ rungs with null pairs $v_{j}, w_{j}$, vacuum idempotent $p_{k} = \prod_{j}w_{j}v_{j}$ and Fock module $F_{k} = B_{k}p_{k}$ of dimension $2^{k}$, with basis the states $v_{S}p_{k}$. With $\tau_{+}$ the reverse and $\tau_{-}$ the reverse composed with the grade involution, $\tau_{\epsilon}(\psi)\phi = \beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, \phi)\,v_{1}\cdots v_{k}$ defines a bilinear form on $F_{k}$ for which every vector is self-adjoint ($\epsilon = +1$, the stored Chevalley pairing) or anti-self-adjoint ($\epsilon = -1$); each is unique up to a factor. It pairs each state with its complement, and it is symmetric or antisymmetric by the sign $\epsilon^{k}(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$, so a symmetric invariant form exists unless $k \equiv 2 \pmod 4$. A symmetric one is neutral, of Witt index $2^{k-1}$: given such a form, the $2^{k}$ states are the vectors of at most $2^{k-1}$ fermionic pairs, never of $2^{k}$.

At three pairs one form is antisymmetric and the other symmetric of signature $(4,4)$, with the two parity halves totally null, so under that form the eight states are the vectors of four pairs. This four is a Witt index; the tower's next floor after one ascent also has four pairs (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tower-is-the-iterated-fock-functor-not-the-ascent}(ii)), an equality of counts that holds only at $k = 3$ and is not an identification: no isometry with the next floor's vector space is compatible with the action of the three-pair algebra, and from four the rule gives eight, not five. At two pairs both forms are antisymmetric. Beside the stored rule of states as creators with new annihilators adjoined ($3, 8, 256, 2^{256}$, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tower-is-the-iterated-fock-functor-not-the-ascent}(i)) this gives a second rule, states as generating vectors under an invariant symmetric form ($k \mapsto 2^{k-1}$: $3, 4, 8, 128, 2^{127}$), which is another reading of the stored phrase (a judgement) and does not reproduce the stored counts. Given the stored bracket of the horizon count, it lies in size between the terms $2^{127}$ and $2^{2^{127}-1}$ of the second rule, a comparison of sizes only, and no stored result is found that selects one (argued, from a search and not an audit).
synthesis.invariant-forms-on-the-fock-mo.lay: The framework's tower is built from pairs of raising and lowering operators, and a system of $k$ pairs has $2^{k}$ basic states. One unproved reading of the tower turns the states of each level into the pairs of the next, which gives the fast-growing counts $3$, $8$, $256$ and then a number near $10^{77}$. This result shows that the count depends on how that step is taken. The states of a level come with a natural way of measuring them against each other, fixed by the algebra itself up to an overall factor. Given that structure, eight states make four pairs, not eight, because each pair needs two of them: the counts then run $3$, $4$, $8$, $128$. The proved tower also goes from three pairs to four, but that is only the same number, and only at three: it is a different construction, and its next step is five where this rule gives eight. Assuming instead that each state becomes one half of a pair and its partner is added from outside gives the faster sequence, which is the one the stored reading quotes. Calling the slower rule a second reading of the same words is a judgement. The two disagree from the second level on. The number of modes on the cosmic horizon is larger than three steps of either and smaller than the next, a comparison of sizes only (that number does not count pairs of this kind), so it cannot tell the rules apart; and, as far as a search of the stored results shows (argued, not a full audit), nothing in the framework selects one.

proofs.main:
Throughout $p = p_{k}$, $\Omega = \Omega_{k}$, $\tau = \tau_{\epsilon}$, and $p' = \prod_{j}v_{j}w_{j}$. The relations give $(w_{j}v_{j})^{2} = w_{j}(1 - w_{j}v_{j})v_{j} = w_{j}v_{j}$ and likewise $(v_{j}w_{j})^{2} = v_{j}w_{j}$; the elements $w_{j}v_{j}$ are even and lie in different planes, so they commute with each other and with $v_{i}, w_{i}$ for $i \ne j$; hence $p$ and $p'$ are idempotents, and $w_{j}p = 0$ because $w_{j}w_{j}v_{j} = Q(w_{j})v_{j} = 0$. Further $v_{j}(w_{j}v_{j}) = (1 - w_{j}v_{j})v_{j} = v_{j}$ and $(v_{j}w_{j})v_{j} = v_{j}$, hence
\[
\Omega p = \Omega = p'\Omega, \qquad \tau(p) = p'
\]
(the reverse of $w_{j}v_{j}$ is $v_{j}w_{j}$, the factors commute, and $p$ is even).

\emph{Relation to the stored pairing.} Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.fock-representation} gives the Fock space as the minimal left ideal on a vacuum idempotent with its occupation basis, and Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.chevalley-pairing} proves, for that model, a nondegenerate form pairing grade $m$ only with grade $k - m$, with symmetry sign $(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$ and every vector self-adjoint; there the creators are the $w_{i}$ and the idempotent is $v_{1}w_{1}\cdots v_{k}w_{k}$, which is the present setting with the two null families exchanged. By the uniqueness proved in (i) below, $\beta_{+}$ is that pairing up to a factor. The proofs of (i) to (iii) are written out in the present notation because $\beta_{-}$, uniqueness and the signature are needed and are not stored.

\emph{The module.} $B_{k}$ is spanned by the products $v_{S}w_{T}$, and $w_{T}p = 0$ unless $T$ is empty, so $F_{k} = B_{k}p$ is spanned by the $v_{S}p$. The map $v_{S} \mapsto v_{S}p$ from the exterior algebra of $W_{k} = \operatorname{span}\{v_{j}\}$ is a nonzero map of $B_{k}$-modules for the Chevalley action ($v_{j}$ by multiplication, $w_{j}$ by the graded derivation with $w_{j}\cdot v_{i} = \delta_{ij}$, which is how $w_{j}$ moves through $v_{S}$ to reach $p$), and that module is irreducible of dimension $2^{k}$ with $B_{k}$ acting as its full endomorphism algebra (Theorem \claimref{tower.fock-module-one-qubit-per-rung}); so the map is an isomorphism and the $v_{S}p$ are a basis.

\emph{(i).} For $\psi = xp$, $\phi = yp$: $\tau(\psi)\phi = p'\,\tau(x)y\,p \in p'F_{k}$. Now $p'v_{S}p = 0$ unless $S$ is the full set: if $j \notin S$, the factor $v_{j}w_{j}$ of $p'$ can be moved next to $v_{S}p$ and $w_{j}v_{S}p = \pm v_{S}w_{j}p = 0$. For the full set $p'\Omega p = \Omega$. So $p'F_{k}$ is the line of $\Omega$, and $\beta_{\epsilon}$ is defined and bilinear. On the basis, $\tau(v_{S}p)v_{T}p = p'\,\tau(v_{S})v_{T}\,p$ and $\tau(v_{S})v_{T} = \pm v_{S}v_{T}$ reordered, which vanishes if $S$ and $T$ meet ($v_{j}^{2} = Q(v_{j}) = 0$), is killed by $p'$ if they do not cover all rungs, and is $\pm\Omega$ if $T = S^{c}$. So the Gram matrix has exactly one nonzero entry, $\pm 1$, in each row and column, and $\beta_{\epsilon}$ is nondegenerate. Since $\tau$ is an antiautomorphism with $\tau(a) = \epsilon a$ on vectors, $\tau(a\psi)\phi = \tau(\psi)\tau(a)\phi = \epsilon\,\tau(\psi)a\phi$, which is the adjoint property. If $\beta'$ is another form with the property, nondegeneracy of $\beta_{\epsilon}$ gives a linear map $L$ of $F_{k}$ with $\beta'(\psi, \phi) = \beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, L\phi)$, and for every vector $a$
\[
\beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, La\phi) = \beta'(\psi, a\phi) = \epsilon\,\beta'(a\psi, \phi) = \epsilon\,\beta_{\epsilon}(a\psi, L\phi) = \beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, aL\phi),
\]
so $L$ commutes with every vector, hence with $B_{k}$, which acts as the full endomorphism algebra of $F_{k}$; $L$ is a scalar.

For $\beta_{-}$: the grade involution $\alpha$ of $B_{k}$ preserves $F_{k}$ ($p$ is even) and acts on $v_{S}p$ by $(-1)^{|S|}$; since $\tau_{-} = \tau_{+}\alpha$, $\tau_{-}(\psi)\phi = \tau_{+}(\alpha\psi)\phi$, that is $\beta_{-}(\psi, \phi) = \beta_{+}(\alpha\psi, \phi)$.

\emph{(ii).} Apply $\tau$ to $\tau(\psi)\phi = \beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, \phi)\Omega$: the left side becomes $\tau(\phi)\psi = \beta_{\epsilon}(\phi, \psi)\Omega$ ($\tau$ is an involution), and $\tau(\Omega) = \epsilon^{k}v_{k}\cdots v_{1} = \epsilon^{k}(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}\Omega$, the reverse of a product of $k$ anticommuting vectors. Hence $\beta_{\epsilon}(\phi, \psi) = \epsilon^{k}(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}\beta_{\epsilon}(\psi, \phi)$. The exponent $k(k-1)/2$ is even exactly for $k \equiv 0, 1 \pmod 4$, and $k(k-1)/2 + k = k(k+1)/2$ exactly for $k \equiv 0, 3$, which gives the table and the two existence statements.

\emph{(iii).} Let $\beta_{\epsilon}$ be symmetric. Since $k \ge 1$, $S \ne S^{c}$, so every basis state is null, and by (i) the plane of $v_{S}p$ and $v_{S^{c}}p$ is hyperbolic and orthogonal to every other basis state. There are $2^{k-1}$ such planes, so the signature is $(2^{k-1}, 2^{k-1})$ and the Witt index $2^{k-1}$; Theorem \claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity} identifies the Witt index with the largest number of mode pairs realised by vectors. For any nondegenerate quadratic form on a space of dimension $2^{k}$ the Witt index is at most half the dimension, which is the last statement. If $\beta_{\epsilon}$ is antisymmetric the same planes are symplectic planes. The form pairs a state of grade $|S|$ only with one of grade $k - |S|$; for odd $k$ these have opposite parity, so each parity half is totally null and the form pairs the halves, and for even $k$ they have equal parity, so the halves are orthogonal and each is nondegenerate.

\emph{(iv).} $s_{+}(3) = (-1)^{3} = -1$ and $s_{-}(3) = (-1)^{3}(-1)^{3} = +1$; (iii) gives signature $(4,4)$ and the null halves, each of dimension $2^{2} = 4$. The vector space of $B_{4} = \Cl(4,4)$ is the orthogonal sum of the four hyperbolic planes of its null pairs, and $(F_{3}, \beta_{-})$ is the orthogonal sum of four hyperbolic planes by (iii), so the two are isometric, as any two hyperbolic spaces of equal dimension are. No isometry intertwines the actions of $B_{3}$. The bivectors of $B_{3}$ act on $F_{3}$ by left multiplication; under them $F_{3}$ is the sum of its two parity halves, and a vector $\psi$ annihilated by all of them is zero: $v_{i}w_{j}\psi = 0$ and $w_{i}v_{j}\psi = 0$ for $i \ne j$ and $(v_{j}w_{j} - w_{j}v_{j})\psi = 0$ force every coefficient of $\psi$ on the basis $v_{S}p$ to vanish (the last relation multiplies $v_{S}p$ by $+1$ if $j \in S$ and $-1$ if not, never by zero; the check computes the common kernel as zero). On the vector space of $B_{4}$, spanned by the vectors of $B_{3}$ and $v_{4}, w_{4}$, the bivectors of $B_{3}$ act by commutator and commute with $v_{4}$ and $w_{4}$, so they annihilate that plane. An intertwining isometry would carry the plane to nonzero annihilated vectors of $F_{3}$, which do not exist. The rule $k \mapsto 2^{k-1}$ gives $8$ at $k = 4$, where the tower's next floor has $5$ pairs. For the equality: $2^{k-1} - (k+1)$ is $-1, -1, 0, 3$ at $k = 1, 2, 3, 4$ and increases by $2^{k-1} - 1 > 0$ at each step from $k = 2$, so it vanishes only at $k = 3$. $s_{+}(2) = -1$ and $s_{-}(2) = (+1)(-1) = -1$, and by the uniqueness in (i) there is no other form for which the vectors are self-adjoint or anti-self-adjoint.

\emph{(v).} The first rule and its counts are Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tower-is-the-iterated-fock-functor-not-the-ascent}(i). The second rule is (iii): a symmetric $\beta_{\epsilon}$ makes $F_{k}$ a hyperbolic space of Witt index $2^{k-1}$, whose Clifford algebra is $\Cl(2^{k-1}, 2^{k-1}) = B_{2^{k-1}}$; $k \mapsto 2^{k-1}$ gives $4$, $8$, $128$, $2^{127}$ from three. At $k = 3$ it must use $\beta_{-}$, the only symmetric form there by (ii) and the uniqueness in (i); every term from the second on is a power of two at least four, so it is divisible by four and both forms are symmetric there by (ii), with the same count; at $k = 2$ no symmetric form exists by (iv). The state counts are $2^{k}$ at $k = 3, 4, 8, 128$, and $3 \times 10^{38} < 2^{128} < 4 \times 10^{38}$. For the horizon count, the bracket $2^{407} < |J| < 2^{408}$ and the rider that sizes only are compared are quoted from Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tower-is-the-iterated-fock-functor-not-the-ascent}(v); given it, compare base-two logarithms: $127 < 407$ and $408 < 2^{127} - 1$. The proved growth is one pair per rung (Theorem \claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity}, and Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exponential-reading-of-the-tower-is-the-iterated-fock-functor-not-the-ascent}(ii) for the ascent from three): $k \mapsto k + 1$ is neither rule, and its value at three equals the second rule's as a number only, by (iv). That the second rule is a reading of the stored phrase is a judgement. The sentence that no stored result selects a rule is argued: the tower results in the store were searched for a statement relating the module of one rung to the generating vectors of a later one, and none was found; this is not an audit of a full cone.

synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground.formal:
Let $T_{k} = \Cl(p{+}k, q{+}k)$, $n = p + q$, $r = p - q$, and let $B_{\infty} \subset \varinjlim T_{k}$ be the subalgebra generated by every plane generator $e_{j}, f_{j}$, $j \ge 1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The relative commutant of $B_{\infty}$ in $\varinjlim T_{k}$ is exactly the even ground algebra $\Cl^{0}(p,q) \subset T_{0}$. On a single floor the commutant of $B_{k}$ is the twisted copy $A_{k} \cong \Cl(p,q)$ of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}, of dimension $2^{n}$; the next plane cuts it to its even half, because the twisted generators $x^{(k)} = x\,\Omega_{k}$ anticommute with $e_{k+1}$ and $f_{k+1}$.
\item[(ii)] So the pair $(\varinjlim T_{k}, B_{\infty})$ determines $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ up to isomorphism and, for $n \ge 1$, hence $n$; the parity of $r$ (the centre of $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ is $\R$ for $n$ odd and $\mathrm{span}\{1, \omega\}$ for $n$ even); for $n$ even, whether $r \equiv 0$ or $2 \pmod 4$ ($\omega^{2} = (-1)^{r/2}$); and, with the types of Theorem \claimref{tower.rigidity-clock-frozen}, the class $\{r, -r\}$ (types $\R \oplus \R$, $\HH \oplus \HH$, $\C$, $\R$, $\HH$ for $r = 0$, $4$, $\pm 2$, $\pm 1$, $\pm 3$).
\item[(iii)] The commutant sees no more than that class: $\Cl^{0}(p,q) \cong \Cl^{0}(q,p)$, the generators $u_{i} = e_{i}e_{n}$ on one frame with every square reversed obeying the same relations.
\end{enumerate}
For $n \ge 1$, at the top of the tower the residue is therefore kept, through the planes' commutant, exactly up to the reversal $r \mapsto -r$, the one symmetry along which Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p2-indifference} equates the towers; whether the pair $(\varinjlim T_{k}, B_{\infty})$ also distinguishes $r$ from $-r$ is not settled here.
synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground.technical: In the infinite tower, the elements that commute with every adjoined plane are precisely the even elements of the ground algebra. On any finite floor more survives: the whole ground algebra appears, twisted by the product of the planes' volume elements, as the commutant of those planes. The next plane removes the twisted odd part, and in the limit, where there is no last plane to supply the twist, only the even ground algebra remains. For $n \ge 1$ the even ground algebra records the dimension, the parity of the charge and, through its type, the residue up to sign; it cannot record the sign, because the even algebras of a signature and of its reverse are isomorphic. This is the residue information that the limit algebra itself, being the same for every tower, cannot carry.
synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground.lay: Each tower starts from a different algebra, but at the top all towers look alike. Some memory of the start survives in how the top is put together: the part of it that is untouched by all the added blocks is the even half of the starting algebra. As long as the starting algebra has at least one generator, that half remembers almost everything about where the tower began, except one mirror-image choice: a tower and its reflected partner leave the same trace. That is exactly the pairing of towers that the dark-matter paper treats as alike.

proofs.main:
\emph{Step 1 (the commutant in the limit).} By the definition of the tower as the chain of unital embeddings $(T_{k}, \iota_{k})$ (\claimref{obj.tower.tower}), every element of its algebraic direct limit, for either parity of $p - q$, lies in some floor and is a combination of finite blades in the ground and plane generators. Conjugation by a generator $g$ acts diagonally on blades, $gB = \pm Bg$, so an element commutes with $g$ exactly when each blade in its support does. For a blade $B$ and a generator $g$ (distinct frame generators anticommute, \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}): if $g \notin B$ then $gB = (-1)^{|B|}Bg$; if $g \in B$ then $gB = (-1)^{|B|-1}Bg$. A blade involves finitely many planes, so some plane generator lies outside it, and commuting with that one forces $|B|$ even; then any plane generator inside $B$ anticommutes with it. So the blades commuting with all of $B_{\infty}$ are the even blades in the ground generators alone, which span $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$. (For $p - q$ even, Theorem \claimref{tower.algebraic-limit-even-charge} identifies the limit further; that is not needed here.)

\emph{Step 2 (the single floor).} On $T_{k}$ the commutant of $B_{k}$ is $A_{k}$, generated by $x^{(k)} = x\,\Omega_{k}$, and $A_{k} \cong \Cl(p,q)$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}). The element $\Omega_{k} = \omega_{1} \cdots \omega_{k}$ is a product of bivectors of the first $k$ planes (Lemma \claimref{tower.volume-elements-planes}), each of which commutes with $e_{k+1}$ and $f_{k+1}$, while $x$ anticommutes with them; so $x^{(k)}$ anticommutes with the new plane, and of $A_{k}$ only the span of products of an even number of twisted generators, which is $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ ($\Omega_{k}^{2} = 1$ and $\Omega_{k}$ commutes with $x$), commutes with $T_{k+1}$'s planes.

\emph{Step 3 (what the commutant records).} For $n$ odd the centre of $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ is $\R$; for $n$ even it is $\mathrm{span}\{1, \omega\}$ with $\omega$ the ground volume element, even and central in $\Cl^{0}$, and $\omega^{2} = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^{q} = (-1)^{r/2}$. Further, $\Cl^{0}(p,q) \cong \Cl(p, q-1)$ (or $\Cl(q, p-1)$) through $e_{i} \mapsto e_{i}e_{n}$, whose type the classification of Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras} gives as listed in (ii), the types that Theorem \claimref{tower.rigidity-clock-frozen} carries unchanged along the tower; the five types are distinct, so with $n$ they fix the class $\{r, -r\}$.

\emph{Step 4 (the reversal).} Reverse every square on one frame. The elements $u_{i} = e_{i}e_{n}$, $i < n$, satisfy $u_{i}^{2} = -Q(e_{i})Q(e_{n})$ and anticommute pairwise, in both signatures, and $Q(e_{i})Q(e_{n})$ is unchanged when both factors change sign. So $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ and $\Cl^{0}(q,p)$ have one presentation and are isomorphic. The check verifies Steps 1 and 2 on small floors (the commutant of all planes of $T_{k+1}$, restricted to $T_{k}$, is the span of the even ground blades; the commutant on $T_{k}$ alone has dimension $2^{n}$), the common presentation of Step 4, and the centre and $\omega^{2}$ of Step 3, in exact arithmetic.
