synthesis.plane-grading-records-residue-.formal:
Let $T_{k} = \Cl(p{+}k, q{+}k)$ be the floors of the tower over $\Cl(p,q)$, $n = p + q \ge 1$, $r = p - q$, with ground generators $x_{1}, \dots, x_{n}$ and planes $(e_{j}, f_{j})$, $e_{j}^{2} = 1$, $f_{j}^{2} = -1$, $j \ge 1$; let $L_{p,q} = \varinjlim T_{k}$ (the real algebraic limit), $B_{\infty} \subset L_{p,q}$ the subalgebra generated by the plane generators, $P_{j} \subset B_{\infty}$ the subalgebra generated by $e_{j}, f_{j}$, and $\alpha_{B}$ the grading of $B_{\infty}$ alone: the automorphism of $B_{\infty}$ that negates every plane generator. Isomorphisms are of real algebras unless stated.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Twisted commutant.)} The set $Z^{1} = \{x \in L_{p,q} : xb = \alpha_{B}(b)x \text{ for all } b \in B_{\infty}\}$ is exactly the odd ground part $\Cl^{1}(p,q) \subset T_{0}$. With the relative commutant $Z^{0} = \Cl^{0}(p,q)$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}, $Z^{0} \oplus Z^{1} = \Cl(p,q)$, a subalgebra graded by this decomposition. So the triple $(L_{p,q}, B_{\infty}, \alpha_{B})$ determines the ground algebra $\Cl(p,q)$ with its grading.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Classification with the plane grading.)} For $n, n' \ge 1$ there is an isomorphism $\Psi \colon L_{p,q} \to L_{p',q'}$ with $\Psi(B_{\infty}) = B_{\infty}$ and $\Psi \circ \alpha_{B} = \alpha'_{B} \circ \Psi$ on $B_{\infty}$ if and only if $n' = n$ and $r' \equiv r \pmod 8$. In particular for $r \not\equiv 0, 4 \pmod 8$ no isomorphism of pairs from the tower over $\Cl(p,q)$ to the tower over $\Cl(q,p)$ respects the planes' grading; the reversal of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-top-pair-forgets-reversal}(i) does not, since it sends the odd generator $e_{2}$ to the even element $e_{1}f_{1}$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Framing.)} For $j \ne k$ the intersection of $P_{j}$ with the commutant of $P_{k}$ is $\mathrm{span}\{1, e_{j}f_{j}\}$, and $\alpha_{B}$ restricted to $P_{j}$ is $\operatorname{Ad}(e_{j}f_{j})$. Hence an isomorphism of pairs that carries each plane $P_{j}$ onto a plane $P'_{\pi(j)}$, with $\pi$ injective, respects the planes' grading, and the framed tower tops obey the classification of (ii): the framing by the individual planes records the sign of $r$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Clocks with no zero mode.)} On the complexification $L_{p,q} \otimes_\R \C$, with $\C$ read as $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ in the second factor (conventions, the unit principle, U1: the scalar $1 \otimes I_4$ commutes with every ground and plane generator by construction, which no element of a floor does, and the odd extensions of U3 do not pass to the limit or exist for odd $n$), let $K_{j} = \tfrac12 e_{j}f_{j}$ and, for real weights $\omega_{j}$, let $\tau_{t} = \operatorname{Ad}\bigl(\exp(t\sum_{j}\omega_{j}K_{j} \otimes I_4)\bigr)$, defined floor by floor (the phase flow of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.phase-flow-is-time-rotor-flow-kms-continuation}(iii), with the scalar $1 \otimes I_4$ in place of that theorem's $J$, since here the unit must also commute with an arbitrary ground; every such clock fixes the ground algebra). Let $\tau'$ be such a clock on the planes of the tower over $\Cl(p',q')$ with \emph{every} weight $\omega'_{j} \ne 0$, for instance the common-rate boost $\kappa K_{\mathrm{tot}}$ or the weights $\omega'_{k} = \kappa k$. If an isomorphism $\Psi \colon L_{p,q} \to L_{p',q'}$ with $\Psi(B_{\infty}) = B_{\infty}$ maps $\Cl(p,q)$ into the fixed points of $\tau'$, which holds in particular when the complexification of $\Psi$ intertwines a clock of the source with $\tau'$, then $\Psi \circ \alpha_{B} \circ \Psi^{-1} = \operatorname{Ad}(c) \circ \alpha'_{B}$ on $B_{\infty}$ for a $\tau'$-invariant invertible $c \in B_{\infty}$ with $c\,\alpha'_{B}(c)$ a positive real number, and $\Psi$ induces a grading-preserving isomorphism $\Cl(p,q) \cong \Cl(p',q')$. Hence $n' = n$ and $r' \equiv r \pmod 8$: for $r \not\equiv 0, 4 \pmod 8$ no isomorphism of pairs from the tower over $\Cl(p,q)$ to the tower over $\Cl(q,p)$ is compatible with a clock that has no zero mode. The hypothesis is sharp: if $\omega'_{1} = 0$, the reversal $\Phi$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-top-pair-forgets-reversal}(i) maps $\Cl(p,q)$ into the fixed points of $\tau'$. When every weight is an odd multiple of one frequency $\omega_{0}$ with $\gcd$ of the multiples $1$, $\tau$ at half its least period $2\pi/\omega_{0}$ is $\alpha_{B}$ itself.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Over $\C$ none of this records the sign.)} The $\C$-linear assignment $x_{i} \mapsto y_{i} \otimes I_4$, every plane generator fixed, is an isomorphism of the complexified limits over $\Cl(p,q)$ and $\Cl(q,p)$ that fixes $B_{\infty, \C}$ pointwise, so it respects the plane grading, every plane and every clock of (iv). The sign of $r$ is recorded by these data only together with the real structure.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.plane-grading-records-residue-.technical: The top of the tower over a signature and over its reversal are isomorphic as algebras with the plane subalgebra marked, through a re-pairing of the planes that mixes even and odd plane elements. This result asks which further datum stops that. The grading of the plane algebra by itself is enough: the elements that anticommute with every plane generator are exactly the odd elements of the ground algebra, and together with the commuting ones, the even ground elements, they rebuild the whole ground algebra $\Cl(p,q)$ with its grading. Since $\Cl(p,q)$ and $\Cl(q,p)$ are different algebras unless $r \equiv 0, 4 \pmod 8$, an isomorphism that respects the planes' grading cannot carry a residue to its reversal; the four-generator shift shows it can still carry $r$ to $r + 8$. Keeping the planes individually supplies the planes' grading, since each plane's even part is what commutes with another plane, so any isomorphism that sends planes to planes respects it. A clock on the planes does almost as much. If every plane turns at a nonzero rate, the clock has a single lowest state on each floor, and the grading acts on that state by a sign; an isomorphism that sends the ground into the clock's fixed points must then twist the planes' grading by an inner automorphism whose square class is positive, which forces the two ground algebras to be isomorphic as graded algebras. The store's reversal escapes only by moving the ground onto a plane generator, which a clock with no zero mode does not leave fixed. When the rates are odd multiples of one frequency the clock at half its period is the grading itself. Over the complex numbers none of this works, because multiplying ground generators by the complexification's unit ($1 \otimes I_4$) reverses their squares while fixing every plane. This covers the I-state's weights $\omega_{k} = \kappa k$ as well as a common rate. A state version (a product Gibbs state of such a clock, whose modular flow is the clock run at $-\beta t$ on each floor) follows if an isomorphism carrying one state to the other intertwines their modular flows on the limit, which standard modular theory gives but which is not proved here.
synthesis.plane-grading-records-residue-.lay: A tower of algebras built over a signature and the tower built over its mirror image have the same top, even when one keeps track of which part of the top came from the added blocks. The earlier result showed this with an explicit relabelling. Here the question is what extra bookkeeping breaks the tie. It is enough to remember, for the added blocks alone, which of their elements count as odd, the property that tells fermions from bosons. That information can be kept by remembering each added block separately, or by running a clock on the blocks in which every block turns at some nonzero rate: the relabelling that swaps a tower for its mirror has to borrow one of the added blocks, and a clock that moves every block leaves none to borrow. With either (for the clock, provided the relabelling sends the starting algebra to elements the clock leaves still), the top remembers whether the tower started from a signature or from its mirror, except for the two residues that are their own mirrors. Over the complex numbers even this is lost, so the distinction lives in the real structure.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} As in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-top-pair-forgets-reversal}, $L_{p,q}$ is the union of the floors, spanned by the finite blades in the ground and plane generators, and conjugation by a generator $g$ acts diagonally on blades: for a blade $B$, $gB = (-1)^{|B|}Bg$ if $g \notin B$ and $gB = (-1)^{|B|-1}Bg$ if $g \in B$ (the blade argument of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}, Step 1). Since $\alpha_{B}$ is an automorphism of $B_{\infty}$ and the plane generators generate $B_{\infty}$, $x \in Z^{1}$ if and only if $xg = -gx$ for every plane generator $g$: if $x$ anticommutes with $g$ and $h$ then $x\,gh = gh\,x = \alpha_{B}(gh)x$, and so on for longer products.

\emph{(i).} Because conjugation by each generator is diagonal on blades, $x \in Z^{1}$ if and only if every blade in its support anticommutes with every plane generator. Let $B$ be such a blade. A blade involves finitely many planes, so some plane generator $h \notin B$, and $hB = -Bh$ forces $|B|$ odd. If some plane generator $g$ lay in $B$, then $gB = (-1)^{|B|-1}Bg = Bg$, a contradiction. So $B$ is an odd blade in the ground generators alone; conversely every such blade anticommutes with every plane generator. Hence $Z^{1} = \Cl^{1}(p,q)$. With $Z^{0} = \Cl^{0}(p,q)$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(i)), $Z^{0} \oplus Z^{1}$ is the span of all ground blades, the subalgebra $\Cl(p,q) = T_{0}$, and the decomposition is its grading. An isomorphism of triples $\Psi$ (with $\Psi(B_{\infty}) = B_{\infty}$, $\Psi\alpha_{B} = \alpha'_{B}\Psi$) maps $Z^{0}$ onto $Z'^{0}$, since $\Psi(B_{\infty}) = B_{\infty}$, and $Z^{1}$ onto $Z'^{1}$: if $xb = \alpha_{B}(b)x$ for all $b$, then $\Psi(x)\Psi(b) = \Psi(\alpha_{B}(b))\Psi(x) = \alpha'_{B}(\Psi(b))\Psi(x)$, and $\Psi(b)$ ranges over $B_{\infty}$; the same with $\Psi^{-1}$ gives equality. So $\Psi$ restricts to a grading-preserving isomorphism $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p',q')$.

\emph{(ii).} If such a $\Psi$ exists, its restriction to the commutants gives $\Cl^{0}(p,q) \cong \Cl^{0}(p',q')$, so $n' = n$ and $r' \equiv \pm r \pmod 8$ by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(ii), and by (i) $\Cl(p,q) \cong \Cl(p',q')$. If $r' \equiv -r$ with $r \not\equiv 0, 4$, then $\Cl(p',q') \cong \Cl(q,p)$ (the real Clifford algebra depends only on $n$ and the residue modulo $8$), and $\Cl(p,q) \not\cong \Cl(q,p)$: the types for $r$ and $-r$ are $\R \oplus \R$ against $\C$ ($r = \pm 1$), $\R$ against $\HH$ ($r = \pm 2$) and $\C$ against $\HH \oplus \HH$ ($r = \pm 3$), Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}. So $r' \equiv r$. An algebra invariant that exhibits the difference without the classification is the signature of the regular trace form $(x,y) \mapsto \operatorname{tr}(L_{xy}) = 2^{n}\br{xy}_{0}$, diagonal on blades with entries $2^{n}B^{2}$; the check computes it for all $n \le 8$ and finds it different for $\Cl(p,q)$ and $\Cl(q,p)$ exactly when $r \not\equiv 0, 4 \pmod 8$. Conversely, for $n' = n$ and $r' \equiv r$, $p' \equiv p \pmod 4$, and the four-generator shift $x_{i} \mapsto x_{i}\omega_{4}$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-top-pair-forgets-reversal}(ii), repeated, is an isomorphism fixing every plane generator, hence $B_{\infty}$ pointwise, hence respecting $\alpha_{B}$. The reversal $\Phi$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-top-pair-forgets-reversal}(i) has $\Phi(e_{2}) = e_{1}f_{1}$ and $\Phi(f_{1}) = e_{1}e_{2}$, even elements, while $\alpha_{B}$ negates $e_{2}$ and $f_{1}$ and fixes $e_{1}f_{1}$, $e_{1}e_{2}$; so $\Phi\alpha_{B} \ne \alpha'_{B}\Phi$.

\emph{(iii).} An element $a + b\,e_{j} + c\,f_{j} + d\,e_{j}f_{j}$ of $P_{j}$ commutes with $e_{k}$ and $f_{k}$, $k \ne j$, if and only if $b = c = 0$, since $e_{j}, f_{j}$ anticommute with them and $1, e_{j}f_{j}$ commute. So, writing $C(\cdot)$ for the commutant in the limit, $P_{j} \cap C(P_{k}) = \mathrm{span}\{1, e_{j}f_{j}\} \cong \R \oplus \R$ ($(e_{j}f_{j})^{2} = -e_{j}^{2}f_{j}^{2} = 1$), whose elements of square $1$ are $\pm 1$ and $\pm e_{j}f_{j}$ (from $(a + d\,e_{j}f_{j})^{2} = a^{2} + d^{2} + 2ad\,e_{j}f_{j}$). Conjugation by $u = e_{j}f_{j}$ ($u^{-1} = u$) negates $e_{j}$ and $f_{j}$ and fixes $1$ and $u$, so $\alpha_{B}|_{P_{j}} = \operatorname{Ad}(u)$. Let $\Psi$ be a pair isomorphism with $\Psi(P_{j}) = P'_{\pi(j)}$, $\pi$ injective. For $j$ pick $k \ne j$; then $\Psi(P_{j} \cap C(P_{k})) = P'_{\pi(j)} \cap C(P'_{\pi(k)})$, the span of $1$ and $u' = e'_{\pi(j)}f'_{\pi(j)}$, so $\Psi(u) = \pm u'$ and, for $b \in P_{j}$, $\Psi(\alpha_{B}(b)) = \Psi(u)\Psi(b)\Psi(u)^{-1} = \operatorname{Ad}(u')(\Psi(b)) = \alpha'_{B}(\Psi(b))$. The $P_{j}$ generate $B_{\infty}$, so $\Psi\alpha_{B} = \alpha'_{B}\Psi$ on $B_{\infty}$, and (ii) applies. The shift fixes every plane, so the framed classification is that of (ii).

\emph{(iv), general clocks.} Write $\alpha$ for $\alpha'_{B}$ on the target and $L' = L_{p',q'}$, with ground generators $y_{1}, \dots, y_{n'}$. Three facts about $B_{\infty}$ are used. (a) It is simple with centre $\R$: it is the union of the floors $B_{k} \cong \Cl(k,k) \cong \Mat_{2^{k}}(\R)$ under unital embeddings, an element central in $B_{\infty}$ is central in some $B_{k+1}$ and so a scalar, and a nonzero two-sided ideal meets some $B_{k}$ in a nonzero ideal, hence contains $1$. (b) $\alpha$ is not inner on $B_{\infty}$: an implementer $d \in B_{k}$ would commute with $e_{k+1}\Omega_{k}$, $\Omega_{k} = \prod_{j \le k}e_{j}f_{j}$, which commutes with $B_{k}$ and is odd. (c) $L' = \bigoplus_{B}y_{B}B_{\infty}$ over the ground blades $y_{B}$, uniquely, and $b\,y_{B} = y_{B}\,\alpha^{|B|}(b)$ for $b \in B_{\infty}$.

Let $\beta = \Psi|_{B_{\infty}}$, an automorphism of $B_{\infty}$, $\tilde\alpha = \beta\alpha_{B}\beta^{-1}$, and $z_{i} = \Psi(x_{i})$. From $x_{i}g = -gx_{i}$ for the plane generators, $z_{i}b = \tilde\alpha(b)z_{i}$ for all $b \in B_{\infty}$. Put $w = z_{1}y_{1}$, invertible; since $y_{1}b = \alpha(b)y_{1}$, $wb = \gamma(b)w$ with $\gamma = \tilde\alpha\alpha$. Expand $w = \sum_{B}y_{B}b_{B}$ by (c): comparing components, $b_{B}b = \alpha^{|B|}(\gamma(b))\,b_{B}$ for every $B$ and $b$. For $b_{B} \ne 0$ the set $B_{\infty}b_{B} = b_{B}B_{\infty}$ is a nonzero two-sided ideal, so $b_{B}$ is invertible by (a) and $\alpha^{|B|}\gamma = \operatorname{Ad}(b_{B})$. If $|B|$ were odd, $\tilde\alpha = \gamma\alpha = \alpha\operatorname{Ad}(b_{B})\alpha = \operatorname{Ad}(\alpha(b_{B}))$ would be inner, and so would $\alpha_{B} = \beta^{-1}\tilde\alpha\beta$, against (b) for the source. So $|B|$ is even, $\gamma = \operatorname{Ad}(c)$ with $c = b_{B}$, and $\tilde\alpha = \operatorname{Ad}(c)\alpha$. Since $\tilde\alpha^{2} = 1$, $\operatorname{Ad}(c\,\alpha(c)) = 1$ and $c\,\alpha(c) = \mu \in \R \setminus \{0\}$ by (a). Then $R_{i} := c^{-1}z_{i}$ satisfies $R_{i}b = \alpha(b)R_{i}$ for all $b \in B_{\infty}$, so $R_{i} \in \Cl^{1}(p',q')$ by (i), and $z_{i} = cR_{i}$ with one $c$ for all $i$.

Now the clock. $z_{i}$ is $\tau'$-fixed and $R_{i}$ is fixed (ground) and invertible, so $\tau'_{t}(c) = c$. Take $k$ with $c \in B_{k}$; on $B_{k}$, $\tau'_{t} = \operatorname{Ad}(\exp(tH_{k} \otimes I_4))$ with $H_{k} = \sum_{j \le k}\omega'_{j}K_{j}$ real, so $c$ commutes with $H_{k}$. The $2K_{j}$ are commuting real involutions; in the irreducible real module of $B_{k}$, of dimension $2^{k}$, each of the $2^{k}$ joint sign patterns occurs exactly once (the $e_{j}$ flip the $j$th sign and fix the others). The least eigenvalue $-\tfrac12\sum_{j \le k}|\omega'_{j}|$ of $H_{k}$ is attained by one pattern only, because no $\omega'_{j}$ vanishes, so its spectral projection $P$, a real polynomial in $H_{k}$, has rank one. $\Gamma_{k} = \prod_{j \le k}e_{j}f_{j} \in B_{k}$ satisfies $\Gamma_{k}^{2} = 1$, commutes with $H_{k}$, and implements $\alpha$ on $B_{k}$; so $\Gamma_{k}P = \eta P$ with $\eta = \pm 1$ and $cP = \nu P$ with $\nu$ real, the range of $P$ being one real line preserved by both. Then $\alpha(c)P = \Gamma_{k}c\Gamma_{k}P = \eta^{2}\nu P = \nu P$ and $\mu P = c\,\alpha(c)P = \nu^{2}P$: $\mu = \nu^{2} > 0$.

So $z_{i}z_{j} = cR_{i}cR_{j} = c\,\alpha(c)R_{i}R_{j} = \mu R_{i}R_{j}$, and the elements $\hat R_{i} = \sqrt{\mu}\,R_{i} \in \Cl^{1}(p',q')$ satisfy $\hat R_{i}^{2} = z_{i}^{2} = x_{i}^{2}$ and anticommute pairwise. The assignment $x_{i} \mapsto \hat R_{i}$ is a grading-preserving homomorphism $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p',q')$; it is injective because $\Psi(x_{B}) = \mu^{\lfloor |B|/2 \rfloor}c^{\,|B| \bmod 2}R_{B}$, so a relation among the $\hat R_{B}$ splits by parity into relations among the $\Psi(x_{B})$; and $n' = n$ by (ii) applied to the commutants, so it is an isomorphism of graded algebras. As in (ii), its even part gives $r' \equiv \pm r$, and for $r' \equiv -r$ with $r \not\equiv 0, 4$ the ungraded types differ, so $r' \equiv r$. Conversely the shifts of (ii) fix every plane and map ground into ground. Sharpness: $\Phi(x_{i}) = y_{i}e_{1}$, and $e_{1}$ commutes with every $K_{j}$, $j \ge 2$, and with $\omega'_{1}K_{1} = 0$; here $c = e_{1}$ has $c\,\alpha(c) = -1 < 0$, the sign the lowest-state argument excludes when no weight vanishes. If $\Psi$ intertwines clocks, $\Psi\tau_{t} = \tau'_{t}\Psi$, then $\Psi(x_{i}) = \Psi(\tau_{t}(x_{i})) = \tau'_{t}(\Psi(x_{i}))$, so the hypothesis holds.

\emph{(iv), half period.} 
On the floor $T_{k,\C}$ put $U_{t} = \exp\bigl(t\sum_{j \le k}\omega_{j}K_{j} \otimes I_4\bigr) = \prod_{j \le k}\bigl(\cos\tfrac{t\omega_{j}}{2} + \sin\tfrac{t\omega_{j}}{2}\,u_{j} \otimes I_4\bigr)$ (the scalar $1 \otimes I_4$ of the complexification, central by construction), $u_{j} = e_{j}f_{j}$, using $u_{j}^{2} = 1$ and that the $u_{j}$ commute. Each $u_{l}$ with $l \ne j$ commutes with $e_{j}, f_{j}$ and with every ground generator, and $u_{j}$ anticommutes with $e_{j}, f_{j}$; so $U_{t}$ commutes with the ground generators and with $K_{l}$ for $l > k$, which makes $\tau_{t} = \operatorname{Ad}(U_{t})$ consistent along the floors, and, writing $c = \cos\tfrac{t\omega_{j}}{2}$, $s = \sin\tfrac{t\omega_{j}}{2}$,
\[
\tau_{t}(e_{j}) = e_{j}(c - s\,u_{j} \otimes I_4)^{2} = \cos(t\omega_{j})\,e_{j} - \sin(t\omega_{j})\,f_{j} \otimes I_4, \qquad \tau_{t}(f_{j}) = \cos(t\omega_{j})\,f_{j} - \sin(t\omega_{j})\,e_{j} \otimes I_4,
\]
($e_{j}u_{j} = f_{j}$, $f_{j}u_{j} = e_{j}$). So $\tau$ fixes the ground algebra, $\tau_{t}$ is the identity on $P_{j}$ exactly when $t\omega_{j} \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, and negates $e_{j}, f_{j}$ exactly when $t\omega_{j} \in \pi + 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$. The flow is the identity at $t$ if and only if $t\omega_{0}m_{j}/2\pi \in \mathbb{Z}$ for every $j$; since $\gcd_{j}m_{j} = 1$ some finite combination $\sum_{j}c_{j}m_{j} = 1$ with integers $c_{j}$, whence $t\omega_{0}/2\pi \in \mathbb{Z}$: the least period is $2\pi/\omega_{0}$. At $t = \pi/\omega_{0}$, $t\omega_{j} = \pi m_{j}$ with $m_{j}$ odd, so $\tau_{\pi/\omega_{0}}$ negates every plane generator: it is $\alpha_{B}$ on $B_{\infty}$, a real automorphism. For the common-rate boost $\kappa K_{\mathrm{tot}}$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.phase-flow-is-time-rotor-flow-kms-continuation}(iii), $K_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_{j}(N_{j} - \tfrac12)$, each $N_{j} - \tfrac12$ is the atom boost $\tfrac12\sigma_{j} = \tfrac12(v_{j}^{*}v_{j} - v_{j}v_{j}^{*})$, which for $v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j})$ and the frame $*$-structure ($e_{j}^{*} = e_{j}$, $f_{j}^{*} = -f_{j}$) is $\tfrac12 e_{j}f_{j} = K_{j}$; so all $m_{j} = 1$. (This reads $v_{j}$ as that theorem's annihilator, $N_{j} = v_{j}^{*}v_{j}$; in the tower's labelling, where $v_{j}$ creates, $N_{j} = v_{j}v_{j}^{*}$ and $N_{j} - \tfrac12 = -K_{j}$, so all $m_{j} = -1$, again odd, and nothing below changes.) If one plane has an even $m_{j}$, $\tau_{\pi/\omega_{0}}$ fixes $P_{j}$ and the half-period map is not the grading; the check shows both cases.

\emph{(v).} With $y_{i}^{2} = -x_{i}^{2}$, $(y_{i} \otimes I_4)^{2} = x_{i}^{2}$ and distinct images anticommute with each other and with the plane generators, so the $\C$-linear assignment extends to a homomorphism of the complexified limits with inverse $y_{i} \mapsto -x_{i} \otimes I_4$; it fixes every plane generator and hence $B_{\infty,\C}$, $\alpha_{B}$, each $P_{j,\C}$ and each $\tau$. It does not preserve the real forms.

The check verifies (i) by enumerating blades on floors $T_{1}, T_{2}$ against the planes of the next floor for ten ground signatures; the trace-form invariant of (ii) for $n \le 8$ and its invariance under the shift; that $\Phi$ sends $e_{2}, f_{1}$ to even elements while the shift fixes every plane; the framing lemma of (iii); the half-period and full-period identities of (iv) with odd and mixed-parity weights, and the lowest-state lemma of (iv): for weights with no zero the least eigenspace of $H_{k}$ has rank one ($2^{k}$ times the scalar part of its projection), $\Gamma_{k}$ acts on it by a sign, and $P\,c\,\alpha(c)\,P = \nu^{2}P$ for invariant $c$ in the commutant of $H_{k}$, while with one zero weight the rank is two and $e_{1}$ is invariant with $e_{1}\alpha(e_{1}) = -1$, in exact arithmetic with complex numbers as pairs of rationals.

synthesis.selector-candidates-on-the-tow.formal:
Notation as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.state-of-a-new-rung-unique-symmetric-extension-is-the-half-weight}: $\Cl_{\Q}(\ell,\ell)$ with generators $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$, ladder pairs $v_{j}$, $w_{j}$ (Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}), tests $\mathrm{on}_{j} = v_{j}w_{j}$, $\mathrm{off}_{j} = w_{j}v_{j}$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generate-the-hyperbolic-plane}), strings $P_{s}$, states under Premise (P) (Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}). An element is \emph{even} if it is a sum of blades of even grade; a state is even if it vanishes on odd elements. A \emph{selector} would have to (a) end interference between the outcomes of a measurement and (b) single out one of them. Four candidates:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Integer states give definiteness only by removing superposition.)} On one rung, the states under (P) with integer values on the blades $1, e, f, fe$ (the ladder's integer form, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.integer-clifford-algebras-contain-no-switch}) are exactly five: on, off, the state of weight $\tfrac12$ vanishing on $e$, $f$, $fe$, and the two states with $\omega(e) = \pm 1$; their weights on the on test are $0$, $1$, $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac12$. The states with integer values on $1, v, w, vw$ (the switch's integer form) are exactly two: on and off. On $m$ rungs, a state with integer values on all products of the $v_{j}$, $w_{j}$ is the state of one string. So in the switch form every state is definite and none has a value strictly between $0$ and $1$ on any test $P_{s}$, or a nonzero value on any $e_{j}$; the tests $\tfrac12(1 \pm e_{j})$ of the rational algebra, which are not in the switch's integer form, get the weight $\tfrac12$. Definiteness holds inside the integer form, interference is absent there altogether, and nothing is selected.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Parity gives two sectors and does not separate records; the stored descent ends interference and does not select.)} The centre of the even subalgebra of $\Cl_{\Q}(n,n)$ is spanned by $1$ and the volume element $\Gamma$ (standard; computed here for $n = 2, 3$): two sectors. A unitary that is even or odd satisfies $\Gamma U = \pm U\Gamma$, so it maps each sector into one sector: the outcomes of a record written by such a coupling on a state in one sector lie in one sector. For the even state on four rungs given by $y = (\tfrac35 v_{1} + \tfrac45 v_{2})\,v_{3}\,P_{0}$ ($P_{0}$ the all-off string) and the even unitary $U = \mathrm{off}_{1} + \mathrm{on}_{1}X$, with $X$ the even self-adjoint element exchanging a quantum between rungs $3$ and $4$, the two records (quantum on rung $4$, quantum on rung $3$) have weights $\tfrac{9}{25}$ and $\tfrac{16}{25}$ and are perfectly correlated with the system's rung; both lie in the same sector of $\Gamma$ and of the total number; and the even self-adjoint element $O = v_{1}w_{2}v_{4}w_{3} + \text{adjoint}$ has value $\tfrac{24}{25}$ in the state after $U$ and $0$ in the state with the interference between the records removed. The same holds for the odd coupling $U'' = \mathrm{off}_{1}e_{4} + \mathrm{on}_{1}e_{3}$ on the state given by $(\tfrac35 v_{1} + \tfrac45 v_{2})P_{0}$: it is unitary, odd, keeps even states even, writes records on single rungs with weights $\tfrac{9}{25}$, $\tfrac{16}{25}$, and the even element $U''(v_{1}w_{2} + \text{adjoint})U''^{\dagger}$ has value $\tfrac{24}{25}$. A coupling that is neither even nor odd, $U' = \mathrm{off}_{1} + \mathrm{on}_{1}e_{3}$, sends an even state to a state that is not even (compare Theorem \claimref{synthesis.records-keep-even-states-even-only-for-parity-homogeneous-observables}). \emph{The stored descent.} The multi-mode descent $\mathcal{E}(x) = \sum_{s}P_{s}xP_{s}$ (Definition \claimref{obj.singularity.multi-mode-descent}) applied to the state after $U$ keeps the record weights $\tfrac{9}{25}$, $\tfrac{16}{25}$ and sends the value of $O$ to $0$: it ends the interference between the records. Applied to the state before any record it sends the value $\tfrac{24}{25}$ of the system's own interference element $v_{1}w_{2} + \text{adjoint}$ to $0$. So requirement (a) is met by a stored map if a premise places it at records and not elsewhere; it gives every record its weight and singles out none.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(No deterministic law on strings.)} On two rungs there is an even rotor $R$ ($R\tilde{R} = RR^{\dagger} = 1$) that takes the state of the string $(1,0)$ to a state with weights $\tfrac{9}{25}$ on $(1,0)$ and $\tfrac{16}{25}$ on $(0,1)$. A map from strings to strings takes a string of weight $1$ to a string of weight $1$. So no rule that assigns to each string one later string reproduces the weights of (P) under even rotors: a law for an actual string on a fixed finite set of rungs, with the string as the only hidden datum, is stochastic, or draws on data outside those rungs.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Unread rungs carry the uniform weight.)} In the one symmetric extension of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.state-of-a-new-rung-unique-symmetric-extension-is-the-half-weight}(ii), applied twice, each of the four strings of the two new rungs has weight $\tfrac14$, and in general $2^{-k}$ on $k$ new rungs. By clause (iii) of that theorem the strings are labels on a finite tower, and a search of the store found no premise that makes one of them actual (a statement about the store, not a computation). The stored account of the tower counts against reading rungs as fresh events: the tower has no clock, and the rungs beyond the first sit on shadow walls away from the physical region (Proposition \claimref{tower.answers-iteration-question}).
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Reading (argued, not proved).} None of the four is a selector on finite towers; the statement is about these four and does not exclude a candidate not listed. (i) gives (b) for free only where (a) is trivial. (ii) shows the one exact superselection rule of a finite tower cannot do (a) for a record written by an even or odd coupling, while the stored descent does (a) wherever it is applied and never (b). (iii) and (iv) together say what a selector on the tower would be: a premise that one string is actual, and a law reading unread rungs, for which (iv) supplies an unbiased prior and nothing else (with a bounded number of rungs read per event such a law gives weights with denominator a power of two only; reading until decided gives any rational weight with a finite number of reads with probability one; argued, standard, not computed here). Those two premises are a theory of the kind of Bell's beables for fermion number; they would make each rung's value a datum, an unbounded list against the short count of free data in Proposition \claimref{one-relation.record-chain-votes-measurement-without-collapse}, and they would depend on the split of (P), which is not preserved by boosts. They are not adopted here. Stochastic collapse and gravitational collapse are further premises of other kinds, not examined beyond naming them.
synthesis.selector-candidates-on-the-tow.technical:
A mechanism for collapse has two jobs: stop the outcomes interfering, and pick one. Four ideas were tried on finite towers, each with a kill condition written first. Requiring whole-number values makes every state a definite string when the integer form is the switch's, but only because nothing else is left: there is no superposition to collapse, and the ladder's integer form keeps three weights, 0, 1/2 and 1. Parity is the one exact superselection rule of a finite tower, with two sectors; a record written by an even or an odd coupling leaves both outcomes in the same sector and an even observable still sees their interference in full. A deterministic rule for an actual string cannot reproduce the weights, since a rotor spreads one string over two. And the unread rungs of the earlier result give every string the same weight, an unbiased prior with no actual value behind it.

So none of the four candidates is a selector on finite towers. The store does hold a map that ends interference, the multi-mode descent, which wipes out interference between occupation records and keeps their weights; applied everywhere it also wipes out the system's own interference before any record, so it would need a premise saying where it acts, and it picks nothing. A selector could be added as two premises (a string is actual; a law reads fresh rungs), and the cost is stated: an unbounded list of data and dependence on a split that boosts change. The result is a survey of named candidates on finite towers, conditional on (P); it is not a proof that no mechanism can exist.
synthesis.selector-candidates-on-the-tow.lay: For a quantum measurement to give one result, something has to stop the possible results from interfering and something has to choose one of them. This result tries four ideas for where the framework might already contain such a chooser, assuming its rule that averages are never negative. If only whole-number values are allowed (in one of the two whole-number versions of the algebra), every state is definite, but only because all the in-between states have been thrown away, which also throws away interference that experiments see. The framework's one exact barrier between kinds of states, parity, has just two sides, and a measurement of the allowed kind leaves both results on the same side, still able to interfere. A fixed rule that moves one definite pattern of switches to another cannot give the right odds. And the fresh switches added by the framework's construction arrive as fair coins with no face showing. So none of these four ideas gives a chooser. The framework does contain a step that stops results interfering, but it treats every result alike and would need a rule saying when it applies. One could be added by assuming that one pattern of switches is real and that fresh switches are read as they arrive, but that is a new assumption with a stated cost, and this result does not make it.

proofs.main:
States, positivity and the adjoint are those of Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}; the pairs are those of Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors} and the tests those of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generate-the-hyperbolic-plane}.

\emph{(i).} A state on one rung is fixed by $a = \omega(e)$, $c = \omega(f)$, $b = \omega(fe)$. Reality gives $c = 0$, since $f^{\dagger} = -f$. With $p = fe$, the elements $e$ and $p$ are self-adjoint, anticommute and square to $1$, so $u = ae + bp$ has $u^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$, and $\omega(x) = 2\langle\rho x\rangle_{0}$ with $\rho = \tfrac12(1 + u)$. If $a^{2} + b^{2} \le 1$ then $\rho$ is a nonnegative combination of the two self-adjoint idempotents $\tfrac12(1 \pm u/|u|)$ over the reals (or $\rho = \tfrac12$ when $u = 0$), so $\omega$ is positive; if $a^{2} + b^{2} > 1$ then $x = u - (a^{2} + b^{2})$ is self-adjoint with $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) = (a^{2} + b^{2})(1 - (a^{2} + b^{2})) < 0$. So positivity is $a^{2} + b^{2} \le 1$; with integer $a$, $b$ this leaves $(0,0)$, $(\pm 1, 0)$, $(0, \pm 1)$, five states, and $\omega(\mathrm{on}) = \tfrac12(1 + b)$. The script finds exactly these five by testing all $27$ integer triples in $\{-1, 0, 1\}^{3}$ against (P) (values outside that range violate $a^{2} + b^{2} \le 1$ or $c = 0$). The ladder's integer algebra is that of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.integer-clifford-algebras-contain-no-switch}. For the switch form, $\omega(vw) = \tfrac12(1 + b)$ and $\omega(v) = \tfrac12(a + c)$ must be integers, so $b = \pm 1$, and then $a = 0$: on and off. On $m$ rungs, the $P_{s}$ are products of the $v_{j}$, $w_{j}$, so an integer-valued state gives them nonnegative integers with sum $1$: one string $s$ has $\omega(P_{s}) = 1$. Then $\omega((1 - P_{s})(1 - P_{s})^{\dagger}) = 0$, and by the Cauchy and Schwarz inequality for the positive form $\omega(xy^{\dagger})$, $\omega(x) = \omega(P_{s}xP_{s})$ for all $x$; since $P_{s}xP_{s}$ is a multiple of $P_{s}$ ($P_{s}$ is a product of one test per rung, and each rung's algebra is the $2 \times 2$ matrices), $\omega$ is the state of the string. Its values on tests are $0$ or $1$ and it vanishes on each $e_{j}$.

\emph{(ii).} The even subalgebra of $\Cl_{\Q}(n,n)$ is generated by the bivectors; an even element commuting with all of them is central in it. $\Gamma$ anticommutes with every generator (the dimension is even), so it commutes with every even element; that the centre is no larger is standard (the even subalgebra is a sum of two matrix algebras), and the script computes the space of even elements commuting with all bivectors as the kernel of a linear map and finds dimension $2$ for $n = 2$ and $n = 3$. A unitary $U$ that is even commutes with $\Gamma$, and one that is odd anticommutes with it; in either case $\Gamma UxU^{\dagger} = \pm U\Gamma xU^{\dagger}$, so $U$ maps the part of a density in one sector into one sector. For the examples the script verifies each stated property exactly. Even coupling: $yy^{\dagger}$ is an even idempotent; $X^{2} = 1$, $X^{\dagger} = X$, $X$ even; $UU^{\dagger} = 1$, $U$ even; the weights $\tfrac{9}{25}$, $\tfrac{16}{25}$ of the two record tests and their perfect correlation with the system's tests; $\Gamma$ acts as the same sign on both record components and the total number is $2$ with zero variance; $O$ is even and self-adjoint with value $\tfrac{24}{25} = 2 \cdot \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac45$, and value $0$ in the state whose density is the sum of the two record-diagonal blocks. Odd coupling: $U''U''^{\dagger} = \mathrm{off}_{1} + \mathrm{on}_{1} = 1$ since $e_{3}^{2} = e_{4}^{2} = 1$ and both commute with the tests of rung $1$; every term of $U''$ is odd; conjugation by an odd element preserves the grading, so even states go to even states; for any even or odd unitary $U$ and any even self-adjoint $O_{0}$, $O = UO_{0}U^{\dagger}$ is even and self-adjoint and has, in the state after $U$, the value $O_{0}$ had before, here $\tfrac{24}{25}$; the script confirms the record weights and that $O$ has value $0$ in the record-diagonal state. For $U'$: it is unitary since $e_{3}^{2} = 1$ and $e_{3}$ commutes with $\mathrm{on}_{1}$; its part $\mathrm{off}_{1}$ is even and its part $\mathrm{on}_{1}e_{3}$ is odd; the script exhibits an even state it sends to a state that is not even, the case of a record of an element that is not parity-homogeneous in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.records-keep-even-states-even-only-for-parity-homogeneous-observables}. The descent: $\mathcal{E}$ of Definition \claimref{obj.singularity.multi-mode-descent} keeps exactly the part of an element diagonal in the strings; the record tests and the $\mathrm{on}_{j}$ are diagonal, so their values are unchanged, while $O$ and $v_{1}w_{2} + \text{adjoint}$ have no diagonal part against a density that $\mathcal{E}$ has made diagonal, so their values become $0$; the script computes $\mathcal{E}$ as the sum over the sixteen strings of four rungs. $\mathcal{E}$ is linear and treats every string alike, so it singles out none.

\emph{(iii).} With $h = v_{1}w_{2} - v_{2}w_{1}$ and $\Pi_{1} = P_{(1,0)} + P_{(0,1)}$, $h^{2} = -\Pi_{1}$ and $h^{\dagger} = -h$, so $R = (1 - \Pi_{1}) + \tfrac35\Pi_{1} + \tfrac45 h$ is even with $RR^{\dagger} = (1 - \Pi_{1}) + (\tfrac{9}{25} + \tfrac{16}{25})\Pi_{1} = 1$, and the script confirms $R\tilde{R} = 1$ and the weights $0, \tfrac{9}{25}, \tfrac{16}{25}, 0$ of $x \mapsto \omega_{(1,0)}(R^{\dagger}xR)$ on the four strings. A function from strings to strings carries the point weight on $(1,0)$ to a point weight; the weights after $R$ are not a point weight.

\emph{(iv).} By clause (ii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.state-of-a-new-rung-unique-symmetric-extension-is-the-half-weight}, the invariant extension vanishes on every blade containing a new generator; applied to two new rungs in turn it is $\omega \otimes$ (the normalised scalar part), and $P_{ab}$ has scalar part $\tfrac14$. Clause (iii) of that theorem is the statement about labels. The statement about the tower's rungs is Proposition \claimref{tower.answers-iteration-question}, clauses 1 and 2.

The Reading is argued from (i) to (iv) and the stored statements it cites; it is not a theorem.

synthesis.state-of-a-new-rung-unique-sym.formal:
Let $A_{\ell} = \Cl_{\Q}(\ell,\ell)$ with generators $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$, $Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$, and ladder pairs $v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j})$, $w_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} - f_{j})$ (Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}). One step of the transport adjoins one hyperbolic plane, unique up to isometry (Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-totality-minimality-completion}): $A_{\ell} \subset A_{\ell+1}$, with new generators $e$, $f$ and new pair $v$, $w$. Write $\mathrm{on} = vw$ and $\mathrm{off} = wv$, the two tests of the new rung (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generate-the-hyperbolic-plane}); $\mathrm{on} + \mathrm{off} = 1$. Assume Premise (P), positivity of values (Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}), for the split $e_{j}, f_{j}$: a \emph{state} is a linear $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$, $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$. An \emph{extension} of a state $\omega$ on $A_{\ell}$ is a state $\Omega$ on $A_{\ell+1}$ with $\Omega = \omega$ on $A_{\ell}$. A \emph{symmetry of the step} is an automorphism of $A_{\ell+1}$ that fixes $A_{\ell}$ pointwise, maps the new plane to itself and commutes with $\dagger$: these are the sign changes $\sigma_{e}$ ($e \mapsto -e$), $\sigma_{f}$ ($f \mapsto -f$) and $\sigma_{e}\sigma_{f}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The completion does not fix the value.)} For every state $\omega$ on $A_{\ell}$ and every $t \in \Q$ with $0 \le t \le 1$ there is an extension $\Omega_{t}$ with $\Omega_{t}(a\,\mathrm{on}) = t\,\omega(a)$ and $\Omega_{t}(a\,\mathrm{off}) = (1 - t)\,\omega(a)$ for $a \in A_{\ell}$, vanishing on $A_{\ell}e$ and $A_{\ell}f$ (the sum $A_{\ell+1} = A_{\ell} \oplus A_{\ell}e \oplus A_{\ell}f \oplus A_{\ell}fe$ is direct, so $a \mapsto a\,\mathrm{on}$ is injective). In particular both the value on ($t = 1$) and the value off ($t = 0$) extend $\omega$. The restriction of $\Omega_{t}$ to the new rung is sharp, that is given by an idempotent, exactly for $t \in \{0, 1\}$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(One symmetric extension.)} $\sigma_{f}$ exchanges $v$ with $w$ and on with off; $\sigma_{e}$ exchanges $v$ with $-w$ and on with off. Among all linear functionals on $A_{\ell+1}$ that restrict to $\omega$, exactly one is invariant under the symmetries of the step: $\Omega_{1/2}$. It is an extension, it gives on and off the weight $\tfrac12$ each, it is not sharp on the new rung, and it takes a value that is not an integer; no extension that is integer valued on the tests, and none that is sharp on the new rung, is invariant (compare Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exchange-of-set-and-clear-is-inner-and-fixed-by-no-integer-state}). \emph{Dependence on the group.} The statement is unchanged if the group is enlarged to all isometries of the new plane: $\Omega_{1/2}$ is also invariant under the boosts $e \mapsto ce + sf$, $f \mapsto se + cf$, $c^{2} - s^{2} = 1$. It fails for smaller groups that do not exchange on with off as a symmetry of the values: under $\sigma_{f}$ alone the invariant extension is not unique, and for $\ell = 0$ the state with $\omega(e) = 1$ is invariant, sharp and integer valued on the blades; under the group generated by the boosts and $\sigma_{e}\sigma_{f}$, which keeps set and clear in their roles, every $\Omega_{t}$ is invariant. So the uniqueness of the half weight needs the exchange of on with off, and a sign change that moves $e$, to count as symmetries of the step; whether they do is a reading, not decided here.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Strings of values are labels, up to one bit.)} On $m$ rungs the $2^{m}$ products of tests $P_{s} = \prod_{j}(\mathrm{on}_{j}$ or $\mathrm{off}_{j})$, $s \in \{0,1\}^{m}$, are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with sum $1$. The sign changes of the $f_{j}$ permute them simply transitively: all $2^{m}$ strings are one orbit of automorphisms that keep the generators up to sign and commute with $\dagger$. Changing two values at once, at rungs $i$ and $j$, is conjugation by the rotor $f_{i}f_{j}$. The volume element $\Gamma = \prod_{j}f_{j}e_{j}$ commutes with every rotor and $\Gamma P_{s} = \pm(-1)^{|s|}P_{s}$ with one overall sign, so under rotors the strings fall into exactly two classes, by the parity of $|s|$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(A string is a weight on one context; whether it extends depends on which elements are tests.)} For two rungs the four $P_{s}$ are one context of atoms in the sense of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.no-two-valued-weights-on-the-atoms-of-two-modes-the-even-subalgebra-admits-them}, on which a string gives the weights $1, 0, 0, 0$; the state of a string gives an atom of another context the weight $\tfrac12$, and that atom is not even. If the atoms of mixed parity are tests, then by clause (i) of that theorem no assignment of the values $0$ and $1$ to all atoms sums to $1$ on every context, so a string cannot be extended to a pre-assignment of an outcome to every test. If only even elements are tests, clause (iii) of the same theorem gives a two-valued additive weight on all self-adjoint idempotents of the even subalgebra of two modes, so there the obstruction is absent.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Reading (argued, not proved).} The question was whether iterating the transport supplies, rung by rung, the fresh bits that a selection of measurement outcomes would need. By (i) the completion forces no value. By (ii) and (iii) it gives the values no meaning beyond a relabelling, except the one class bit of the whole string, a chirality bit of the same kind as the stored orientation bit (that it is that bit is not shown); the only extension it singles out is the unbiased one, which has no value and exists only once $\tfrac12$ does. By (iv) a string taken as data could not fix outcomes test by test if tests of mixed parity are allowed, and could for even tests on two modes. So on every finite tower, and with the exchange counted as a symmetry, iteration supplies two-state systems and no bits of data; the infinite tower is not treated here. A selector built on the tower would need a further premise: that each rung's value is a datum, with a law reading it. The weight $\tfrac12$ equals the stored occupation of a boundary mode at zero weight; that is recorded as an observation.
synthesis.state-of-a-new-rung-unique-sym.technical:
A transport step adds one hyperbolic plane, hence one two-state system, to the algebra. Under the premise (P) on values, a state on the old algebra extends to the enlarged one with any weight between 0 and 1 on the new rung's "on" test, so the completion does not decide whether the new rung is on or off. The step has symmetries, the sign changes of the two new generators, which leave the old algebra and the adjoint of (P) alone; one of them exchanges set with clear. Exactly one extension is symmetric under these sign changes (and under all isometries of the new plane): the one with weight one half on each value. If the exchange is not counted as a symmetry this fails: under the sign change of one generator alone a sharp invariant state exists, and under the boosts with the joint sign change every weight is invariant. It is not sharp and not integer valued. For several rungs, the strings of on and off values are all carried into one another by such sign changes, and pairs of changes are rotations, so the only thing about a string that a rotation cannot change is the parity of the number of rungs that are on: one bit, a chirality bit of the same kind as the store's orientation bit. Finally a string is a yes-or-no assignment on one set of mutually exclusive tests; the stored result on two-valued weights shows it cannot be continued to all tests if tests of mixed parity are allowed, and can be for even tests on two modes.

The result is conditional on (P) and on the reading of "symmetry of the step" as the sign changes of the new generators. It is algebra on finite towers; the infinite tower and laboratory records are not treated. It does not exclude a selector of outcomes; it shows that iteration alone is not one.
synthesis.state-of-a-new-rung-unique-sym.lay: Each step of the framework's basic construction adds one new on-off switch. The question was whether these switches, added without end, could be the hidden source of the random-looking outcomes of quantum measurements: perhaps each new switch arrives already on or already off, and those settings decide what we see. Assuming the framework's rule that averages can never be negative, this result shows the construction does not decide the setting of a new switch: on and off are both allowed, and so is anything in between. If swapping on with off counts as a symmetry of the construction, the only arrangement that respects it is the fifty-fifty one, which has no definite setting at all; if it does not count, this conclusion fails. For many switches, any pattern of settings can be turned into any other by relabelling, apart from one overall yes-or-no fact that the framework already counts once. And a pattern of settings could fix the answers to all measurements in advance only if measurements are restricted to a special kind (those that do not mix even and odd). So, for any finite number of switches, adding switches gives a supply of coins, not a supply of results of coin tosses. The case of infinitely many switches is not settled here. To make the switches decide outcomes one would have to add a new assumption saying so.

proofs.main:
Throughout, $p = fe$ for the new plane, so $\mathrm{on} = vw = \tfrac12(1 + p)$ and $\mathrm{off} = wv = \tfrac12(1 - p)$; $p$ is even, $p^{2} = 1$, $p^{\dagger} = e^{\dagger}f^{\dagger} = -ef = p$, and $p$ commutes with $A_{\ell}$ (it is a product of two vectors orthogonal to the generators of $A_{\ell}$). The pair $v$, $w$ is a switch (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generate-the-hyperbolic-plane}), the adjunction of the plane is the step of Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-totality-minimality-completion}, and the pairs are those of Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}.

\emph{(i).} States, positivity and reality are those of Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}. As a vector space $A_{\ell+1} = A_{\ell} \oplus A_{\ell}e \oplus A_{\ell}f \oplus A_{\ell}p$. Every $a \in A_{\ell}$ commutes with $\mathrm{on}$ and $\mathrm{off}$; $e\,\mathrm{on} = \mathrm{off}\,e$ and $f\,\mathrm{on} = \mathrm{off}\,f$, so $\mathrm{on}\,e\,\mathrm{on} = \mathrm{on}\,f\,\mathrm{on} = 0$; and $p\,\mathrm{on} = \mathrm{on}$. Hence for $x = a + be + cf + dp$,
\[
\mathrm{on}\,x\,\mathrm{on} = E_{1}(x)\,\mathrm{on}, \qquad E_{1}(x) := a + d \in A_{\ell},
\]
and likewise $\mathrm{off}\,x\,\mathrm{off} = E_{0}(x)\,\mathrm{off}$ with $E_{0}(x) = a - d$. Put $\Omega_{1} = \omega \circ E_{1}$, $\Omega_{0} = \omega \circ E_{0}$ and $\Omega_{t} = t\,\Omega_{1} + (1 - t)\,\Omega_{0}$, that is $\Omega_{t}(x) = \omega(a) + (2t - 1)\omega(d)$. Then $\Omega_{t} = \omega$ on $A_{\ell}$, $\Omega_{t}(1) = 1$, $\Omega_{t}$ vanishes on $A_{\ell}e$ and $A_{\ell}f$, and $\Omega_{t}(a\,\mathrm{on}) = \tfrac12\omega(a) + \tfrac12(2t - 1)\omega(a) = t\,\omega(a)$, likewise for off. Reality: $\mathrm{on}$ is self-adjoint, so $E_{1}(x^{\dagger})\,\mathrm{on} = (\mathrm{on}\,x\,\mathrm{on})^{\dagger} = E_{1}(x)^{\dagger}\,\mathrm{on}$, and $\omega$ is real. Positivity: with $1 = \mathrm{on} + \mathrm{off}$,
\[
\mathrm{on}\,xx^{\dagger}\,\mathrm{on} = (\mathrm{on}\,x\,\mathrm{on})(\mathrm{on}\,x\,\mathrm{on})^{\dagger} + (\mathrm{on}\,x\,\mathrm{off})(\mathrm{on}\,x\,\mathrm{off})^{\dagger} .
\]
Since $f$ is $e\,p$ up to a sign and $p\,\mathrm{off} = -\mathrm{off}$, $\mathrm{on}\,x\,\mathrm{off} = g\,e\,\mathrm{off}$ for some $g \in A_{\ell}$ (a combination of $b$ and $c$), and $(g\,e\,\mathrm{off})(g\,e\,\mathrm{off})^{\dagger} = g\,e\,\mathrm{off}\,e\,g^{\dagger} = g\,\mathrm{on}\,g^{\dagger} = gg^{\dagger}\,\mathrm{on}$. So $E_{1}(xx^{\dagger}) = E_{1}(x)E_{1}(x)^{\dagger} + gg^{\dagger}$ and $\Omega_{1}(xx^{\dagger}) = \omega(E_{1}(x)E_{1}(x)^{\dagger}) + \omega(gg^{\dagger}) \ge 0$; the same for $\Omega_{0}$, and a convex combination of states is a state. For $t$ outside $[0, 1]$, $\Omega_{t}(\mathrm{on}\,\mathrm{on}^{\dagger}) = t$ or $\Omega_{t}(\mathrm{off}\,\mathrm{off}^{\dagger}) = 1 - t$ is negative. The script confirms positivity exactly, as positive semidefiniteness of the Gram matrix $\Omega_{t}(e_{S}e_{T}^{\dagger})$ on all blades, for $\ell = 1, 2$, two states $\omega$ and three values of $t$, and its failure for $t = -\tfrac15$ and $t = \tfrac65$. On the new rung $\Omega_{t}$ is given by the element $t\,\mathrm{on} + (1 - t)\,\mathrm{off}$, whose square is $t^{2}\mathrm{on} + (1 - t)^{2}\mathrm{off}$: idempotent exactly for $t \in \{0, 1\}$.

\emph{(ii).} A sign change of generators extends to an automorphism of the Clifford algebra; $\sigma_{e}$, $\sigma_{f}$ fix the generators of $A_{\ell}$, hence $A_{\ell}$ pointwise, and commute with $\dagger$ because $\dagger$ is defined generator by generator. $\sigma_{f}(v) = \tfrac12(e - f) = w$, so $\sigma_{f}(\mathrm{on}) = wv = \mathrm{off}$; $\sigma_{e}(v) = \tfrac12(-e + f) = -w$ and $\sigma_{e}(\mathrm{on}) = (-w)(-v) = \mathrm{off}$. On the summands: $\sigma_{e}$ negates $A_{\ell}e$ and $A_{\ell}p$, $\sigma_{f}$ negates $A_{\ell}f$ and $A_{\ell}p$. A linear functional invariant under both therefore vanishes on $A_{\ell}e \oplus A_{\ell}f \oplus A_{\ell}p$, and if it restricts to $\omega$ it is $a + be + cf + dp \mapsto \omega(a)$, which is $\Omega_{1/2}$. This uses no positivity: uniqueness holds among all linear functionals. $\Omega_{1/2}(\mathrm{on}) = \tfrac12$, not an integer; by (i) it is not sharp on the new rung; and an extension with $\Omega(\mathrm{on}) \in \{0, 1\}$ or integer valued on the tests differs from $\Omega_{1/2}$, so is not invariant. \emph{Dependence on the group.} A boost fixes $A_{\ell}$, maps $A_{\ell}e \oplus A_{\ell}f$ to itself and fixes $p$ (it has determinant $1$ on the plane), so every $\Omega_{t}$, which vanishes on $A_{\ell}e \oplus A_{\ell}f$, is invariant under it; in particular $\Omega_{1/2}$ is invariant under every isometry of the plane, the group generated by the boosts, $\sigma_{e}$ and $\sigma_{f}$. A boost with $c + s = 2$ sends $v$ to $2v$ and $w$ to $\tfrac12 w$, and $\sigma_{e}\sigma_{f}$ sends $v, w$ to $-v, -w$: these keep on and off, so under the group they generate every $\Omega_{t}$ is invariant. Under $\sigma_{f}$ alone, which fixes $e$, a functional may be nonzero on $A_{\ell}e$: for $\ell = 0$ the functional of $\tfrac12(1 + e)$, a self-adjoint idempotent, is a state, is invariant, is sharp and has integer values $1, 1, 0, 0$ on $1, e, f, fe$. The script checks these statements exactly for the boost with $c = \tfrac54$, $s = \tfrac34$. This is the one-switch case of clause (v) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exchange-of-set-and-clear-is-inner-and-fixed-by-no-integer-state}, here relative to a given state on the rungs below.

\emph{(iii).} The tests of different rungs commute and $\mathrm{on}_{j}\mathrm{off}_{j} = 0$, so the $P_{s}$ are orthogonal idempotents; expanding $\prod_{j}(\mathrm{on}_{j} + \mathrm{off}_{j}) = 1$ gives the sum. The sign change of $f_{j}$ exchanges $\mathrm{on}_{j}$ and $\mathrm{off}_{j}$ and fixes the other rungs' tests, so the group $(\Z/2)^{m}$ of these sign changes acts on the strings by flipping entries: simply transitively. For $i \ne j$ the element $R = f_{i}f_{j}$ is even with $R\tilde{R} = f_{i}f_{j}f_{j}f_{i} = 1$; it anticommutes with $f_{i}$ and $f_{j}$ and commutes with every other generator, so $x \mapsto Rx\tilde{R}$ is the sign change of $f_{i}$ and $f_{j}$ together. The volume element $\Gamma$ anticommutes with every generator (the dimension $2m$ is even), hence commutes with every even element and so with every rotor; $p_{j}\,\mathrm{on}_{j} = \mathrm{on}_{j}$ and $p_{j}\,\mathrm{off}_{j} = -\mathrm{off}_{j}$ give $\Gamma P_{s} = \pm(-1)^{m - |s|}P_{s}$ with the sign of the ordering of $\Gamma$. If $P_{s'} = RP_{s}\tilde{R}$ for a rotor $R$ then $\Gamma P_{s'} = R\Gamma P_{s}\tilde{R}$ has the same sign, so strings of different parity are not conjugate under rotors, and strings of equal parity differ by an even number of flips, a product of the rotors above. So there are exactly two classes.

\emph{(iv).} For two rungs each $P_{s}$ is self-adjoint with scalar part $\tfrac14$, the four are orthogonal and sum to $1$: a context of the atoms of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.no-two-valued-weights-on-the-atoms-of-two-modes-the-even-subalgebra-admits-them}, and the state $x \mapsto \langle P_{s}x\rangle_{0}/\langle P_{s}\rangle_{0}$ of a string gives it the weights $1, 0, 0, 0$. With $y = P_{s} + v_{j}P_{s}$ for a rung $j$ that is off in $s$, $\Pi = \tfrac12 yy^{\dagger}$ is a self-adjoint idempotent to which the string's state gives $\tfrac12$ (computed by the script for one string). The element $y$ has a part of each parity, so $\Pi$ is not even. Clause (i) of the cited theorem says no function from the atoms to $\{0, 1\}$ sums to $1$ on every context, and its eighteen atoms are not all even; a string determines such a function on one context and so has no extension of that kind when atoms of mixed parity are tests. Clause (iii) of the same theorem gives a two-valued additive weight on the self-adjoint idempotents of the even subalgebra of two modes, which is the stated exception.

The script checks exactly: (i) for $\ell = 1, 2$ as described; (ii) the action of the three symmetries on the old blades, on $\dagger$, on $v$ and on the tests, that every blade containing a new generator is negated by one of them, the values of $\Omega_{1/2}$ on all blades, that among five values of $t$ only $\tfrac12$ is invariant, and the idempotent test; (iii) for $m = 3$: the eight idempotents, the simply transitive action, the three rotors, the commutation of $\Gamma$ with all fifteen bivectors and the four-four split of its signs; (iv) the context, the weights of a string and the weight $\tfrac12$ on an atom outside it.

synthesis.tower-limit-forgets-residue.formal:
Let $L_{p,q} := \varinjlim T_{k}$ be the algebraic limit of the tower over $\Cl(p,q)$ (\claimref{obj.tower.tower}), $n = p + q$, $r = p - q$, with ground frame $x_{1}, \dots, x_{n}$ ($x_{i}^{2} = +1$ for $i \le p$, $-1$ for $i > p$) and planes $(e_{j}, f_{j})$, $e_{j}^{2} = 1$, $f_{j}^{2} = -1$, $j \ge 1$. Write $H_{\infty} := H_{1} \perp H_{2} \perp \cdots$, so that $L_{0,0} = \Cl(H_{\infty})$, and $B_{\infty} \subset L_{p,q}$ for the subalgebra generated by the planes.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For every $(p,q)$, with $r$ of either parity, $L_{p,q} = \Cl(\R^{p,q} \perp H_{\infty})$ and
\[
L_{p,q} \;\cong\; \Cl(H_{\infty}) \;\cong\; \Mat_{2^{\infty}}.
\]
An isomorphism $\Phi \colon L_{p,q} \to L_{0,0}$ is the extension of the frame bijection $x_{i} \mapsto e_{i}$ ($i \le p$), $x_{p+i} \mapsto f_{i}$ ($i \le q$), $e_{j} \mapsto e_{p+j}$, $f_{j} \mapsto f_{q+j}$; it carries $T_{k}$ into the floor $T'_{k + \max(p,q)}$ of the tower over $\Cl(0,0)$, and for $n \ge 1$ it does not carry $B_{\infty}$ onto the plane subalgebra of $L_{0,0}$, which is all of $L_{0,0}$. The algebra $L_{p,q}$ therefore determines neither $n$ nor $r$.
\item[(ii)] For $r$ even, with Theorem \claimref{tower.algebraic-limit-even-charge}: $\Cl(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}} \cong \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$, the ground algebra being absorbed whether it is of type $\Mat_{k}(\R)$ or $\Mat_{k}(\HH)$.
\item[(iii)] For $r$ odd, $L_{p,q} \cong \Cl^{0}(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$, where $\Cl^{0}(p,q) \cong \Cl(p, q-1)$ if $q \ge 1$ and $\Cl^{0}(p,0) \cong \Cl(0, p-1)$, both of even residue; and $L_{p,q}$ is \emph{not} isomorphic to $\Cl(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$. For a finite-dimensional $A$ the centre of $A \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$ is $Z(A) \otimes 1$; it is $\R$ for $L_{p,q}$, and for $A = \Cl(p,q)$ it is the two-dimensional centre $\R \oplus \R$ or $\C$ of Lemma \claimref{tower.grade-twist-when-it-inner}. Each finite floor $T_{k}$ has the two-dimensional centre $\mathrm{span}\{1, \omega_{T_{k}}\}$, and of it only $\R$ commutes with the next plane.
\item[(iv)] For the frame $*$-structure of Lemma \claimref{tower.structure-tower-c-norms}, the complexification of $\Phi$ is a $*$-isomorphism. Hence for every $(p,q)$ the complexified limit carries a unique C*-norm, and its completion is the CAR algebra, the completion of $L_{0,0}^{\C}$ by Theorem \claimref{tower.car-limit-even-charge} at $p = q = 0$.
\end{enumerate}
So for odd charge the limit is again a plain tensor product with $\Mat_{2^{\infty}}$, of the even ground algebra $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ rather than of $\Cl(p,q)$, and no invariant of the algebra, real K-theoretic or other, separates residues or dimensions. What the top of the tower keeps of the residue is carried by the planes' subalgebra $B_{\infty}$, whose relative commutant is $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}).
synthesis.tower-limit-forgets-residue.technical: The limit of the tower over $\Cl(p,q)$ is the Clifford algebra of an infinite quadratic space with countably many orthonormal vectors of each sign. Any two such spaces are isometric: list the positive vectors of each in one sequence and the negative vectors in another, and match the lists. So every tower's limit, whatever its ground signature, is the same algebra, the Clifford algebra of countably many hyperbolic planes, which is the algebraic $2^{\infty}$ matrix algebra. The matching shifts the planes along to make room for the ground generators, so it moves floors upwards and does not respect the planes' subalgebra; the bare algebra forgets the dimension and the residue. For even residue this shows that tensoring with $\Mat_{2^{\infty}}$ absorbs the ground algebra, quaternionic type included. For odd residue the limit is $\Cl^{0}(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$ and not $\Cl(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$: the centre of a tensor product with $\Mat_{2^{\infty}}$ is the centre of the finite factor, which is one-dimensional for the limit but two-dimensional for odd $\Cl(p,q)$. At each finite floor the volume element is central, but the next plane anticommutes with it, so the centre dies in the limit. The matching respects the adjoint of the frame, so after complexification every limit completes to the same CAR algebra. The residue survives at the top of the tower only through the planes' subalgebra, whose commutant is the even ground algebra.
synthesis.tower-limit-forgets-residue.lay: The series builds, over every starting algebra, an infinite ladder by adding one pair of opposite directions at each rung. For starting algebras of one kind the series knew what the top of the ladder is; for the other kind it was an open question. The answer is that the top is the same in every case: with infinitely many rungs there is always room to relabel, so the starting directions are absorbed into the rungs. Which tower one started from is not visible in the top as a bare algebra; it is visible only if one also remembers which part of the top came from the rungs.

proofs.main:
\emph{Step 1 (the limit is a Clifford algebra, for either parity).} By the definition of the tower (\claimref{obj.tower.tower}), $T_{k} = \Cl(V_{k})$ with $V_{k} = \R^{p,q} \perp H_{1} \perp \cdots \perp H_{k}$, and $\iota_{k}$ is induced by the inclusion $V_{k} \subset V_{k+1}$ (\claimref{std-algebra.functoriality}); each $\iota_{k}$ carries the blade basis of $T_{k}$ into that of $T_{k+1}$ and is injective. Every element of $L_{p,q}$ lies in some floor, so $L_{p,q}$ is generated by its frame $\mathcal{F} = \{x_{i}\} \cup \{e_{j}, f_{j}\}$. We use the universal property of each floor (\claimref{std-algebra.existence-uniqueness}): if $g_{1}, \dots, g_{N}$ is the orthonormal frame of $T_{k}$ and $y_{1}, \dots, y_{N}$ are elements of a unital algebra with $y_{a}^{2} = g_{a}^{2}$ and $y_{a}y_{b} = -y_{b}y_{a}$ for $a \ne b$, there is a unique unital homomorphism $T_{k} \to$ that algebra with $g_{a} \mapsto y_{a}$. The argument of the second paragraph of the proof of Theorem \claimref{tower.algebraic-limit-even-charge}, which does not use the parity of $p - q$, identifies $L_{p,q}$ with $\Cl(\R^{p,q} \perp H_{\infty})$; the steps below need only the universal property of the floors.

\emph{Step 2 (the frame bijection, (i)).} Let $\sigma$ be the bijection of (i) from $\mathcal{F}$ to the frame $\mathcal{F}' = \{e'_{j}, f'_{j}\}$ of $L_{0,0}$: it lists the positive generators $x_{1}, \dots, x_{p}, e_{1}, e_{2}, \dots$ in order onto $e'_{1}, e'_{2}, \dots$ and the negative generators $x_{p+1}, \dots, x_{n}, f_{1}, f_{2}, \dots$ in order onto $f'_{1}, f'_{2}, \dots$. It preserves squares, and distinct frame elements of $\mathcal{F}'$ anticommute, so for each $k$ the images of the frame of $T_{k}$ satisfy the relations of that frame, and the universal property gives $\Phi_{k} \colon T_{k} \to L_{0,0}$. The images lie in $T'_{k + \max(p,q)}$, since $x_{i} \mapsto e'_{i}$ with $i \le p$, $x_{p+i} \mapsto f'_{i}$ with $i \le q$, $e_{j} \mapsto e'_{p+j}$ and $f_{j} \mapsto f'_{q+j}$ with $j \le k$. As $\Phi_{k+1} \circ \iota_{k}$ and $\Phi_{k}$ agree on the frame of $T_{k}$, they are equal, and the $\Phi_{k}$ assemble to $\Phi \colon L_{p,q} \to L_{0,0}$. In the same way $\sigma^{-1}$ gives $\Psi \colon L_{0,0} \to L_{p,q}$, carrying $T'_{k}$ into $T_{k}$. Then $\Psi\Phi$ and $\Phi\Psi$ are unital homomorphisms fixing every frame element, and the limits are generated by their frames, so both are identities: $\Phi$ is an isomorphism. By Theorem \claimref{tower.algebraic-limit-even-charge} at $p = q = 0$, $L_{0,0} \cong \Cl(0,0) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}} = \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$, and $L_{0,0} = \Cl(H_{\infty})$ by Step 1. For $n \ge 1$, $B_{\infty}$ is the span of the blades in plane generators alone, so $x_{1} \notin B_{\infty}$ by linear independence of blades and $B_{\infty} \ne L_{p,q}$; the plane subalgebra of $L_{0,0}$ is all of $L_{0,0}$, and $\Phi$ is bijective, so $\Phi(B_{\infty}) \ne L_{0,0}$. Since the algebras $L_{p,q}$ for all $(p,q)$ are isomorphic to one algebra, the algebra alone determines neither $n$ nor $r$.

\emph{Step 3 ((ii)).} For $r$ even, Theorem \claimref{tower.algebraic-limit-even-charge} gives $L_{p,q} \cong \Cl(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$, and (i) gives $L_{p,q} \cong \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$. The even residues are of types $\Mat_{k}(\R)$ ($r \equiv 0, 2$) and $\Mat_{k}(\HH)$ ($r \equiv 4, 6$), and both are absorbed.

\emph{Step 4 ((iii)).} Let $r$ be odd, so $n$ is odd and $n \ge 1$. If $q \ge 1$, put $u_{i} = x_{i}x_{n}$ for $i < n$, with $x_{n}^{2} = -1$: then $u_{i}^{2} = -x_{i}^{2}x_{n}^{2} = x_{i}^{2}$ and $u_{i}u_{j} = -u_{j}u_{i}$ for $i \ne j$, so the universal property gives a homomorphism $\Cl(p, q-1) \to \Cl^{0}(p,q)$; it is onto, since $u_{i}u_{j} = -x_{n}^{2}\,x_{i}x_{j}$ gives $x_{i}x_{j} = -x_{n}^{2}\,u_{i}u_{j}$ for $i, j < n$ ($x_{n}^{2} = \pm 1$), and $x_{i}x_{n} = u_{i}$, while every even blade is a product of such pairs; and both sides have dimension $2^{n-1}$, so it is an isomorphism. If $q = 0$, then $x_{n}^{2} = +1$, $u_{i}^{2} = -x_{i}^{2} = -1$, and the same argument gives $\Cl^{0}(p,0) \cong \Cl(0, p-1)$. The residues $r + 1$ and $1 - p$ are even. Write $(p', q')$ for the signature obtained. By (i) twice and Theorem \claimref{tower.algebraic-limit-even-charge} for the even residue,
\[
L_{p,q} \;\cong\; \Mat_{2^{\infty}} \;\cong\; L_{p',q'} \;\cong\; \Cl(p', q') \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}} \;\cong\; \Cl^{0}(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}.
\]
For the centre: $A \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$ is the increasing union of $A \otimes \Mat_{2^{k}} = \Mat_{2^{k}}(A)$ along $z \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(z, z)$. A central $z$ lies in some $\Mat_{2^{k}}(A)$ and commutes with the real matrix units of $\Mat_{2^{k}}(\R) \subset \Mat_{2^{k}}(A)$, which forces $z = \operatorname{diag}(a, \dots, a) = a \otimes 1$; commuting with $A \otimes 1$ forces $a \in Z(A)$. Conversely $Z(A) \otimes 1$ commutes with the generating subalgebras $A \otimes 1$ and $1 \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$. So $Z(A \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}) = Z(A) \otimes 1 \cong Z(A)$. For $L_{p,q} \cong \R \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$ this is $\R$. For $A = \Cl(p,q)$ with $r$ odd, Lemma \claimref{tower.grade-twist-when-it-inner} gives the centre $\R \oplus \R$ or $\C$, of dimension $2$. Isomorphic algebras have isomorphic centres, so $L_{p,q} \not\cong \Cl(p,q) \otimes \Mat_{2^{\infty}}$. On the floors: $T_{k}$ has odd dimension $n + 2k$, so its volume element $\omega_{T_{k}}$ commutes with every vector of $V_{k}$ and is central, and the centre of $T_{k}$ is $\mathrm{span}\{1, \omega_{T_{k}}\}$: the same lemma applied to $T_{k}$, whose residue is again $r$, gives a two-dimensional centre, which contains this two-dimensional span. The generator $e_{k+1}$ is orthogonal to all $n + 2k$ factors of $\omega_{T_{k}}$, so it anticommutes with it, and $a + b\,\omega_{T_{k}}$ commutes with $e_{k+1}$ only for $b = 0$.

\emph{Step 5 ((iv)).} The frame $*$ of Lemma \claimref{tower.structure-tower-c-norms} is the conjugate-linear antiautomorphism with $g^{*} = g$ for frame generators of square $+1$ and $g^{*} = -g$ for those of square $-1$, compatible with the $\iota_{k}$, hence defined on the complexified limits. Since $\sigma$ preserves squares, $\Phi^{\C} \circ *$ and $* \circ \Phi^{\C}$ are conjugate-linear antihomomorphisms agreeing on the frame, so they are equal: $\Phi^{\C}$ is a $*$-isomorphism $L_{p,q}^{\C} \to L_{0,0}^{\C}$. A C*-norm on $L_{p,q}^{\C}$ is carried by $\Phi^{\C}$ to a C*-norm on $L_{0,0}^{\C}$, and $p - q = 0$ is even, so by Lemma \claimref{tower.structure-tower-c-norms} there is exactly one; hence $L_{p,q}^{\C}$ carries exactly one C*-norm, and $\Phi^{\C}$ extends isometrically to the completions. The completion of $L_{0,0}^{\C}$ is $\Cl(0,0)_{\C} \otimes \CAR = \CAR$ by Theorem \claimref{tower.car-limit-even-charge}.

\emph{The closing sentence.} By (i) to (iii) the algebra is the same for every $(p,q)$, so no invariant of it separates the cases. Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(i) identifies the relative commutant of $B_{\infty}$ in $L_{p,q}$ as $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ for either parity of $r$, so the pair $(L_{p,q}, B_{\infty})$, unlike the algebra, keeps information about the residue.

The check verifies on truncations, in exact arithmetic, that the frame bijection respects squares and anticommutation and the floor bookkeeping, with $\Psi\Phi$ the identity on generators; the presentation of $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ as $\Cl(p,q-1)$ or $\Cl(0,p-1)$ for odd $n$; and, for odd $r$, that the centre of each floor is spanned by $1$ and the floor's volume element while the elements of a floor commuting with the next floor's generators are the scalars.
